between the applicant Couples and the couples "married" by the MCCT,
on the one hand, and heterosexual couples, on the other hand, on the basis of
their personal characteristics, i.e., their sexual orientation. Secondly, the
claimants are subject to differential treatment on the basis of a ground of
discrimination which has been held to be a ground analogous to those enumerated
in
s. 15
, namely, sexual orientation. Finally, the differential treatment of
the claimants discriminates against them in a substantive sense, bringing into
play the purpose of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
in remedying such ills as
prejudice, stereotyping and historical disadvantage: see, Law v. Canada
(Minister of Employment and Immigration), supra, per Iacobucci J. at p. 524
S.C.R., adopted by Cory J. and Iacobucci J. in M. v. H., supra, at pp. 46-47
S.C.R.

[
83
] The evidence supports a conclusion that "marriage" represents
society's highest acceptance of the self-worth and the wholeness of a couple's
relationship, and, thus, touches their sense of human dignity at its core.
[page362]

[
84
] The equality provisions of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
are therefore
violated.

The Section 1 Justification

[
85
] Although I am more inclined than LaForme J. to the view that a s. 1
analysis is required when considering the constitutionality of a common law
rule in circumstances such as this, he conducted such an analysis in any event,
and I agree with his reasoning in that analysis.

[
86
] There are indications in Supreme Court of Canada jurisprudence that a
s. 1 analysis may not always be appropriate where what is involved is a
Charter

challenge to a common law, judge-made rule: see, for example, R. v. Swain,

1991 CanLII 104 (SCC)
, [1991] 1 S.C.R. 933, 63 C.C.C. (3d) 481; Canadian Broadcasting Corp. v.
Dagenais,
1994 CanLII 39 (SCC)
, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 835, 120 D.L.R. (4th) 12. Nonetheless, s. 1 analyses
were conducted in both of those cases; and in Hill v. Church of Scientology of
Toronto,
1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130, 126 D.L.R. (4th) 129, Cory J. carefully drew a
distinction between circumstances in which the constitutionality of government
action is challenged and those which involve a Charter challenge to the common
law in private litigation (see pp. 1169-72 S.C.R.). In the latter situation --
of which Hill was an example -- "the balancing must be more flexible than the
traditional s. 1 analysis undertaken in cases involving governmental action
cases" (p. 1171 S.C.R.).

[
87
] The applications before this court involve a
Charter
challenge to a
common law rule establishing the definition of "marriage", on the
basis of which the action of government in refusing to issue marriage licences
and to register marriages performed under the publication of church banns is
contested. In such circumstances, it is my view that the conduct of a s. 1 type
of analysis is preferable.

[
88
] In any event, given the views I have expressed regarding the broader
approach to the institution of marriage which is required of the law in
present-day Canada, and for the reasons expressed by Justice LaForme in his
judgment, I am satisfied that the common law definition of marriage cannot
withstand a s. 1 Oakes analysis. [See Note 19 below]

[
89
] As a result, I conclude that the common law definition of marriage --
excluding same-sex couples from access to that institution, as it does --
cannot stand. [page363]

[
90
] This brings me, then, to the difficult question of the proper remedy to
be applied in the circumstances of this case in order to give effect to that
conclusion.

IV. REMEDY

[
91
] As indicated, Justice LaForme has concluded the appropriate remedy in
the circumstances is for the court, itself, to reformulate the common law rule
of marriage as the lawful and voluntary union of one man and one woman to the
exclusion of all others. LaForme J. would simply redefine the common law rule
by substituting the words "two persons" for the words "one man
and one woman" in the foregoing definition.

[
92
] Respectfully, I disagree with this direct approach.

[
93
] In my opinion, the appropriate remedy in these circumstances is to
strike down the common law definition of marriage and declare it
constitutionally invalid and inoperative. However, I would suspend the
operation of the declaration of invalidity for a period of 24 months to enable
Parliament (with the legislatures, where applicable) to correct the violation and
bring the impugned law into line with the constitutional requirements of the

Charter
. Finally, in the event that Parliament (with the legislatures, where
applicable) fails to do so, I would declare the common law respecting marriage
to be reformulated in the fashion suggested by Justice LaForme. My reasons for
arriving at these conclusions follow.

[
94
] I find the question of the appropriate remedy to be applied in the
circumstances of this case most difficult. While the conclusion that Justice
LaForme has reached in this regard has much to commend it -- given his
determination of the other issues, with which, as I have said, I agree -- I
believe, with utmost deference to my colleague, that it is the primary
responsibility of Parliament (with the legislatures, where necessary), and not
of the courts, to reformulate the definition of marriage. They have the better
capacity to do so, and are accountable directly to the public. They should be
afforded the opportunity.

[
95
] In a constitutional democracy such as Canada, it is the legislature
(comprised of the elected legislative and executive branches of government)
which should assume the major responsibility for law reform. Major revisions of
legal rules -- including the common law -- with complex and uncertain
ramifications, are therefore best left to Parliament and the legislatures, and
courts (the appointed third branch of government) should be reluctant to change
the law themselves unless the contemplated change is an incremental one.
Legislatures are better equipped to make complex [page364] social policy
decisions. See, for example, M. v. H.,
1999 CanLII 686 (SCC)
, [1999] 2 S.C.R. 3 at pp. 59-60, paras.

78-81
, 171 D.L.R. (4th) 577, per Iacobucci J.

[
96
] This approach is mandated, in my opinion, not only when the court is
conducting its s. 1 analysis of the infringement in question in order to
determine whether a law can survive
Charter
scrutiny, but also when the court
is considering the appropriate remedy to be put in place.

[
97
] The linguistic change proposed seems simple and straightforward enough
on its face. It may even follow logically from the earlier conclusions I have
drawn. However, the consequences and potential reverberations flowing from such
a transformation in the concept of marriage, it seems to me, are extremely
complex. They will touch the core of many people's belief and value systems,
and their resolution is laden with social, political, cultural, emotional and
legal ramifications. They require a response to a myriad of consequential
issues relating to such things as inheritance and property rights, filiation,
alternative biogenetic and artificial birth technologies, adoption and other
marriage- status driven matters. The courts are not the best equipped to
conduct such a balancing exercise, in my opinion.

[
98
] This is not an incremental change in the law. It is a profound change.

[
99
] Although there may be historical examples of the acceptance of same-sex
unions, everyone acknowledges that the institution of marriage has been
commonly understood and accepted for centuries as the union of a man and a
woman. Deep- seated cultural, religious and socio-political mores have evolved
and shaped society's views of family, child-rearing and protection and
"couple-hood" based upon that heterosexual view of marriage. The
apparent simplicity of a linguistic change in the wording of a law does not
necessarily equate with an incremental change in that law. To say that altering
the common law meaning of marriage to include same-sex unions is an incremental
change, in my view, is to strip the word "incremental" of its
meaning.

[
100
] An authoritative articulation of the constitutional- democracy
deference principle is found in the following statement of McLachlin J. in
Watkins v. Olafson,
1989 CanLII 36 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 750 at pp. 760-61, 61 D.L.R. (4th) 577:

This branch of the case . . . raises starkly the
question of the limits on the power of the judiciary to change the law.
Generally speaking, the judiciary is bound to apply the rules of law found in
the legislation and in the precedents. Over time, the law in any given area may
change; but the process of change is a slow and incremental one, based largely
on the mechanism of extending an existing principle to new circumstances. While
it may be that some judges are more activist than others, the courts have
generally declined to introduce major and far-reaching changes in the rules
hitherto accepted as governing the situation before them. [page365]

There are sound reasons supporting this judicial
reluctance to dramatically recast established rules of law. The court may not
be in the best position to assess the deficiencies of the existing law, much
less problems which may be associated with the changes it might make. The court
has before it a single case; major changes in the law should be predicated on a
wider view of how the rule will operate in the broad generality of cases.
Moreover, the court may not be in a position to appreciate fully the economic
and policy issues underlying the choice it is asked to make. Major changes to
the law often involve devising subsidiary rules and procedures relevant to
their implementation, a task which is better accomplished through consultation
between courts and practitioners than by judicial decree. Finally, and perhaps
most importantly, there is the long-established principle that in a
constitutional democracy it is the legislature, as the elected branch of the
government, which should assume the major responsibility for law reform.

Considerations such as these suggest that major
revisions of the law are best left to the legislature. Where the matter is one
of a small extension of existing rules to meet the exigencies of a new case and
the consequences of the change are readily assessable, judges can and should
vary existing principles. But where the revision is major and its ramifications
complex, the courts must proceed with great caution.

(Emphasis added)

See also, R. v. Hawkins,
1996 CanLII 154 (SCC)
, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 1043, 141 D.L.R. (4th) 193, per
Lamer C.J. and Iacobucci J., at pp. 1071-73 S.C.R.

[
101
] Watkins v. Olafson was not a
Charter
infringement case. It involved
the application of a long-standing common law rule in personal injury cases
that called for the payment of a lump sum amount on account of future losses.
However, the cautionary principles articulated above by McLachlin J. have been
acknowledged in various other authorities in which Charter considerations were
at stake, including cases where the inconsistency of the common law with
Charter values was being considered: see, for example, R. v. Salituro,
1991 CanLII 17 (SCC)
, [1991] 3
S.C.R. 654 at p. 670, 68 C.C.C. (3d) 289; M. v. H., supra, at p. 86 S.C.R.;
Hill v. Church of Scientology, supra, at p. 1171 S.C.R.

[
102
] In Salituro, at p. 670 S.C.R., Iacobucci J. observed:

These cases reflect the flexible approach that
this court has taken to the development of the common law. Judges can and
should adapt the common law to reflect the changing social, moral and economic
fabric of the country. Judges should not be quick to perpetuate rules whose
social foundation has long since disappeared. Nonetheless, there are
significant constraints on the power of the judiciary to change the law. As
McLachlin J. indicated in Watkins, supra, in a constitutional democracy such as
ours it is the legislature and not the courts which has the major
responsibility for law reform; and for any changes to the law which may have
complex ramifications, however necessary or desirable such changes may be, they
should be left to the legislature. The judiciary should confine itself to those
incremental changes which are necessary to keep the common law in step with the
dynamic and evolving fabric of our society.

[Emphasis added] [page366]

And at p. 675 S.C.R.:

Where the principles underlying a common law rule
are out of step with the values enshrined in the
Charter
, the courts should
scrutinize the rule closely. If it is possible to change the common law rule .
. . without upsetting the proper balance between judicial and legislative
action that I have referred to above, then the rule ought to be changed.

(Emphasis added)

[
103
] Should this court decide to change the common law definition of
marriage peremptorily by reformulating it to include the union of same-sex
couples, without first affording Parliament (and, where applicable, the
legislatures) an opportunity to deal with the matter, the court would, in my
view, be "upsetting the proper balance between judicial and legislative
action" that should prevail in this country. This is so, "however
necessary or desirable such changes may be".

[
104
] The applicants rely upon the following comments of Iacobucci J. (on
behalf of himself and Cory J.), in Vriend v. Alberta,
1998 CanLII 816 (SCC)
, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 493, 156
D.L.R. (4th) 385, to the effect that "governmental incrementalism"
cannot provide a justification for
Charter
violations (at pp. 559-60 S.C.R.):

In addition, in Egan, writing on behalf of myself
and Cory J., I took the position that the need for governmental incrementalism
was an inappropriate justification for
Charter
violations. I remain convinced
that this approach is generally not suitable for that purpose, especially
where, as here, the statute in issue is a comprehensive code of human rights
provisions. In my opinion, groups that have historically been the target of
discrimination cannot be expected to wait patiently for the protection of their
human dignity and equal rights while governments move toward reform one step at
a time. If the infringement of the rights and freedoms of these groups is
permitted to persist while governments fail to pursue equality diligently, then
the guarantees of the Charter will be reduced to little more than empty words.

(Emphasis added)

[
105
] I do not read this statement as undermining the general principles
calling for courts to exercise caution in changing the law and to respect the
balance between the role of the courts and legislative bodies, and the dynamic
of dialogue existing between them in that regard. For one thing, Justice
Iacobucci, himself, had reiterated those very principles earlier in Salituro, as
cited above, and he recognized them again in M. v. H., supra (p. 87 S.C.R.)
released about a year after Vriend. Moreover, he said as much, as well, in
Vriend itself, when he noted that "in fashioning a remedy with regard to a

Charter
violation, a court must be mindful of the role of the legislature"
(para. 137), and when he commented (at para. 136) that:

In carrying out their duties, courts are not to
second-guess legislatures and the executives; they are not to make value
judgments on what they regard as [page367] the proper policy choice; this is
for the other branches. Rather, the courts are to uphold the Constitution and
have been expressly invited to perform that role by the Constitution itself.
But respect by the courts for the legislature and executive role is as
important as insuring that the other branches respect each other's role and the
role of the courts.

(Emphasis added)

[
106
] The judiciary's role as guardian of the Constitution is to uphold the
principles and values underlying and enunciated in the Constitution and
Charter

by ensuring that the laws of this country are consistent with those principles
and values. If they are not, then -- to the extent they are inconsistent --
they are of no force and effect:
Constitution Act, 1982, s. 52(1)
. The court's
remedial power in the event of a violation is broad and flexible but, in my
opinion, must be exercised with a keen eye on the policy of restraint reflected
in the jurisprudence reviewed above. The potential remedies are to be applied
in a fashion which demonstrates both respect for the purposes of the Charter
and for the role of the legislature by avoiding undue intrusion into the
legislative sphere: see, Schachter v. R.,
1992 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 679, 93 D.L.R. (4th)
1.

[
107
] If the infringing law can be remedied by a simple incremental change
with foreseeable results, without impinging upon the role of the legislature,
judges should act to fill the gap created by the violation. In my opinion,
however, where the potential ramifications of the change required to make an
impugned law consistent with constitutional and
Charter
values are extensive
and uncertain, and where they evoke socio- political, cultural, economic,
religious and moral debate of the sort the legislature is more suited to
address, it is incumbent upon the judiciary to adhere to the principles
outlined above, and not simply to pay lip service to them -- regardless of
one's personal view of the appropriate outcome.

[
108
] The temptation to act positively -- and to correct the wrong as well
as to strike it down -- is strong. The plight and the needs of the individual
litigants whose case is the vehicle through which the impugned law is being
tested, are often heartfelt, poignant and distressing. They cry out for an
immediate remedy. Such is the case here. Judges, like others, may think they
have the easy and correct answer to complex social problems, and that reading
down the law or reading in a few words to change the law so that it complies
with constitutional and
Charter
principles will settle the issue as it should
be and get the job done without further delay.

[
109
] That, however, is not our role in my opinion. Members of the judiciary
are appointed to uphold the Constitution and to ensure that the laws of this
country measure up against the values and principles underlying and enunciated
in the Constitution and the
Charter
. Major changes and reforms to the law are
the [page368] responsibility of the legislature, whose members are elected to
perform those functions. To reiterate what McLachlin J. said in Watkins, supra,
"there are sound reasons supporting this judicial reluctance to
dramatically recast established rules of law."

[
110
] This approach balances the respective roles of the branches of
government and promotes the kind of dialogue between the courts and legislative
bodies recently underlined in such cases as Reference re Secession of Quebec,

1998 CanLII 793 (SCC)
, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 217, 161 D.L.R. (4th) 385 and Corbière v. Canada (Minister of
Indian and Northern Affairs),
1999 CanLII 687 (SCC)
, [1999] 2 S.C.R. 203, 173 D.L.R. (4th) 1. As noted
by L'Heureux-Dubé J. in Corbière (p. 283 S.C.R.):

The link between public discussion and
consultation and the principles of democracy was recently reiterated by this
court in Reference re Secession of Quebec,
1998 CanLII 793 (SCC)
, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 217, at para.
68
:
"a functioning democracy requires a continuous process of
discussion". The principle of democracy underlies the Constitution and the

Charter
, and is one of the important factors guiding the exercise of a court's
remedial discretion. It encourages remedies that allow the democratic process
of consultation and dialogue to occur.

[
111
] When a law is measured against the benchmark of
Charter
values and
found to be wanting, the courts are cautious about rewriting statutes and
reformulating principles of common law to amend or replace that law. This is
particularly so where the ramifications of the change required are far-reaching
and uncertain, and where the change touches diverse but deeply-held values and
mores of a socio-political, cultural and religious nature. Here, it is not
simply a matter of filling in a gap left in the common law by a finding of
constitutional invalidity. It is a matter of crafting a solution that bridges a
chasm of community, social and moral principles.

[
112
] This bridge must be built. But in my opinion, it is not only the role
but the obligation of Parliament (and, where applicable, of the legislatures)
to build it, and to craft a solution that will survive
Charter
scrutiny.

[
113
] In Schachter v. Canada, supra, Chief Justice Lamer introduced his
analysis of remedial options to address
Charter
infringements with the
following remark (at p. 695 S.C.R.):

A court has flexibility in determining what
course of action to take following a violation of the
Charter
which does not
survive s. 1 scrutiny.
Section 52
of the Constitution Act, 1982 mandates the
striking down of any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the
Constitution, but only "to the extent of the inconsistency".
Depending upon the circumstances, a court may simply strike down, it may strike
down and temporarily suspend the declaration of invalidity, or it may resort to
the techniques of reading down or reading in. In addition,
s. 24
of the Charter
extends to any court of competent jurisdiction the power to grant an
"appropriate and just" remedy to "[a]nyone whose [Charter]
rights and freedoms . . . have been infringed or denied". In choosing how
to apply
s. 52
or
s. 24
[page369] a court will determine its course of action
with reference to the nature of the violation and the context of the specific
legislation under consideration.

[
114
] As previously noted, I have concluded the appropriate remedy in this
case is to strike down the impugned common law rule defining marriage as the
union of one man and one woman, and to temporarily suspend the declaration of
invalidity, rather than to resort to the technique of reading out/reading in in
order to reformulate the common law rule.

[
115
] The Schachter decision is instructive because Chief Justice Lamer
outlined a series of propositions which he said were intended to operate as
"guidelines to assist courts in determining what action under
s. 52
is
most appropriate in a given case". These propositions are developed at
length at pp. 702-17 S.C.R. of the judgment, and summarized at pp. 717-19
S.C.R. In brief, the suggested general format for the courts to follow is this:

(a) First, the court should consider the extent of the inconsistency between
the
Charter
right infringed and the legislative provision that must be struck
down. Usually the manner in which the law violates the Charter and the manner
in which it fails to be justified under s. 1 will be relevant to this
determination.

(b) Secondly, the court should consider the type of remedy which is
appropriate -- severance, reading in, or striking down -- keeping in mind what
Chief Justice Lamer termed "the twin guiding principles", namely,
respect for the role of the legislature, on the one hand, and respect for the
purposes of the
Charter
, on the other. Severance or reading in will only be
warranted in the clearest of cases

(p. 718 S.C.R.). Factors to be canvassed in this regard include such things as,

-- remedial precision (i.e., the extent to which
the remedy can be achieved with precision, while avoiding undue intrusion into
the legislative sphere);

-- interference with the legislative objective
(would severance or reading-in entail such an intrusion into the spheres of
legislative objectives and legislative budgetary policy as to change the nature
of the legislative scheme in question?); and,

-- the impact of the proposed remedy on the
surviving portion of the legislation (as severed, or as altered by reading-down
or reading-in). [page370]

(c) Finally, having identified the extent of the inconsistency in question
and determined whether that inconsistency should be dealt with by way of
striking down, severance, or reading in, the final step is for the court to
determine whether the declaration of invalidity should be temporarily
suspended. A court should only suspend a declaration of constitutional
invalidity where striking down a provision immediately would pose a danger to
the public, would threaten the rule of law, or, due to a finding of
underinclusiveness, would deprive deserving (and already included) persons of a
benefit without thereby benefiting those wrongly excluded, in light of whether
or not there is an obligation to provide the benefit at all.

[
116
] These propositions were developed in the context of a statutory
violation of the
Charter
. Nonetheless -- and although they are not a perfect
fit -- they are relevant and helpful in considering the appropriate remedy in a
case involving a common law principle that is inconsistent with the Charter.

[
117
] In the present applications, the nature of the violation in question
is the underinclusiveness of the common law definition of marriage. It excludes
same-sex unions. Once it is accepted that heterosexual procreation is not the
determining feature of marriage in modern society, the objective of preserving
the institution of marriage for male/ female unions only is no longer pressing
and substantial and cannot justify overriding the applicants'
s. 15
rights.
Thus, the first part of the Oakes test is not met. Nor is there any rational
connection between the objective of the institution and the gender or sexual
preferences of its members. Therefore, the first part of the proportionality
test in Oakes is not met either. In short, the extent of the inconsistency
between the requirements of the
Charter
and the common law rule is
considerable.

[
118
] I do not think the "remedial precision" aspect of the
Schachter guidelines permitting severance/reading in is met in the
circumstances of this case, however. Remedial precision does not mean, simply,
ease of exchange between the language to be severed and the language to be
inserted -- here, the sought- after exchange of the words "two
persons" for the words "one man and one woman". Remedial
precision has to do with whether the objective of the legislation (or, in this
case, the common law) can be met with the least interference and without
unacceptable intrusion into the legislative domain (p. 718 S.C.R.). The
following passage from the judgment of Lamer C.J. accents this point (p. 705
S.C.R.):

While reading in is the logical counterpart of
severance, and serves the same purposes, there is one important distinction
between the two practices [page371] which must be kept in mind. In the case of
severance, the inconsistent part of the statutory provision can be defined with
some precision on the basis of the requirements of the Constitution. This will
not always be so in the case of reading in. In some cases, the question of how
the statute ought to be extended in order to comply with the Constitution
cannot be answered with a sufficient degree of precision on the basis of
constitutional analysis. In such a case, it is the legislature's role to fill
in the gaps, not the court's.

(Emphasis added)

[
119
] In my view that is the situation here: "the question of how [the
common law] ought to be extended in order to comply with the Constitution
cannot be answered with a sufficient degree of precision on the basis of
constitutional analysis", and "it is [Parliament's] role to fill in
the gaps, not the court's."

[
120
] The debate starts on the footing that the required change in the law
is in sharp contrast to Parliament's present -- and clearly expressed -- choice
regarding marriage. It is evident that Parliament's current approach to the institution
is rooted in the common law definition: see the
Modernization of Benefits and
Obligations Act
, supra,
s. 1.1
; the
Federal Law -- Civil Law Harmonization Act,
No. 1, S.C. 2001, c. 4, ss. 5
-
7
; Parliamentary Motion, House of Commons
Debates, 1st sess., 36th Parl., vol. 135 at 15960-93, 16034-36, and 16068-69 (8
June 1999). I do not accept, however, that Parliament will not change its views
in the face of the newly declared unconstitutionality of the common law rule,
and will engage in what the applicants fear will be an approach of
"remedial evasion". The MBOA is itself an indication of Parliament's
willingness to legislate in response to required, albeit contentious,
constitutional change. The fact that the change respecting the concept of
marriage, required by this ruling, is in such contrast to Parliament's current
views is a factor in favour of providing Parliament with an opportunity to
craft its own solution to the problem, rather than a factor in favour of
directly imposing a judge-made rule on Parliament, in my opinion.

[
121
] There are legislative offshoots of this constitutionally mandated
change -- actual and potential -- which should be kept in mind as well.
Although various pieces of omnibus legislation enacted by Parliament and the
provinces in the wake of the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in M. v. H.,
have extended benefits and obligations to same-sex couples on the same basis as
opposite-sex couples in a wide variety of situations -- the
MBOA
, itself,
amended 69 federal statutes -- there remain areas where benefits and
protections are still a function of male/female-spouse language. Differences in
the treatment of same-sex and opposite-sex partners remain in such federal
spheres as the way in which the testimony of spousal-like partners is dealt
with under the
Canada Evidence Act
[page372] and the way in which sponsorship
applications are handled under the Immigration Act and Regulations. As well, in
Ontario at least, certain benefits continue to be enjoyed exclusively by
opposite-sex married couples under the statutory regimes governing family law
rights to property and equalization, and the law of estates and succession.
[See Note 20 below] There may be considerations relating to the changes in
these spheres consequent upon the inclusions of same-sex unions in the
institution of marriage which need to be addressed simultaneously with a
recognition of that inclusion, which the court cannot foresee and with which
Parliament and the legislatures will be required to deal. This factor also militates
towards legislative deference from the court in these circumstances, in my
view.

[
122
] As I have suggested, the ramifications of the change required to bring
the law into conformity with
Charter
rights and values are potentially
extensive and, to some extent, uncertain. They will evoke robust
socio-political, cultural, economic, religious and moral debate. In short,
democratic debate will ensue. Parliament is the forum for that type of
discussion and for the balancing of such conflicting societal interests. It
should be accorded some flexibility in dealing with contentious and
morally-laden issues: see Rodriguez v. British Columbia (Attorney General),

1993 CanLII 75 (SCC)
, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 519 at p. 614, 107 D.L.R. (4th) 342; R. v. Hess,
1990 CanLII 89 (SCC)
, [1990] 2
S.C.R. 906, 59 C.C.C. (3d) 161; Vriend, supra, p. 564 S.C.R.

[
123
] Much evidence was put before us to demonstrate the diversity of views
in society about "same-sex marriage". I have recited some of this
evidence at the outset of these reasons. This is particularly true of the religious
community, which has an [page373] intense interest in the subject, and a broad
range of tenaciously held -- and often conflicting -- views as to how the issue
should be resolved. As one Roman Catholic observed, "all Canadians,
whatever their belief set, have a stake in the nature of so foundational a
social institution as marriage, with its implications for both adults and
children as well as for the functioning of society generally." [See Note
21 below]

[
124
] At one end of this spectrum of debate, conservative Catholic, Islamic
and Evangelical Protestant clergy, and some academics, have expressed concerns
that if the state recognizes same-sex marriages, their faiths will feel
excluded from an institution which they hold to be fundamental in their world
view of society. They worry that some may feel required to refrain from
performing marriage ceremonies because the institution of marriage will have
become antithetical to their beliefs. They query whether clergy could continue
to act as agents of the state as marriage celebrants while at the same time
refusing to perform same-sex marriages. Still others are concerned about the
exclusionary affects on their very cultures in society.

[
125
] Finally, there is evidence from social and religious historians such
as Professor Edward Shorter, [See Note 22 below] and Professor Katherine Young
articulating the view that the inclusion of same-sex unions in marriage may
undermine and diminish the institution of marriage altogether, with unforeseen
unfavourable consequences for society. In support of these concerns, Professor
Young theorizes that changing the universal features of marriage could lead to
increased polarization of men and women and/or to an identity crisis for men.
Professor Shorter and Professor Douglas Allen [See Note 23 below] also argue
the experience with no-fault divorce shows that there can be significant
unanticipated and unintended consequences of radical changes to social
institutions -- not all negative, but often unfavourable. [page374]

[
126
] While I do not accept these opinions as establishing a justifiable
basis for sustaining the institution of marriage as a heterosexual preserve, I
do think they buttress the argument that Parliament should craft the solution
for putting the required change into effect.

[
127
] This brings me to my final consideration respecting remedy in this
case.

[
128
] Although reformulating the concept of civil marriage to replace the
union of "one man and one woman" with the union of "two
persons" is obviously a leading alternative for consideration in bringing
the law into line with
Charter
values, it is not the only option.

[
129
] The example most commonly put forward is the "registered domestic
partnership" regime which has been implemented in various northern European
countries, [See Note 24 below] and in the State of Vermont, and the Province of
Nova Scotia. Since the argument of these applications -- on June 7, 2002 -- the
National Assembly of Quebec passed a "Civil Union" Bill. [See Note 25
below] A registered partnership model allows same-sex partners (and in some
cases, opposite-sex partners) to register their relationship with the state.
Registration brings with it most of the rights and duties of marriage, but
provides a "parallel" recognition of the relationship, leaving
"marriage" to opposite-sex couples. There are variations between
regimes. Some have restrictions with respect to adoption, filiation and
biogenetic reproduction.

[
130
] Like Justice LaForme, I have some concerns about the adequacy of the
registered domestic partnership regime to meet the requirements of the
Charter
.
Equality of benefits and protection are not necessarily the same thing as full
and equal recognition. Having said that, however, this court does not have
before it a legislatively enacted registered partnership scheme for
consideration and measurement against the requirements of the Constitution and
the Charter. Accordingly, I do not think the court can, or should, effectively
judge that question in advance and out of context.

[
131
] There is another option as well. The notion of civil marriage could be
replaced altogether, and "marriages" left to be [page375] performed
by the various religious institutions in accordance with their faith-based
traditions and conscience. Instead of civil marriage, there might be a system
of "legal civil unions" into which both opposite-sex and same-sex
couples who take part in a form of religious marriage are required to enter.
Such a civil union could also be open to couples who choose not to go through a
religious marriage, but who wish to formalize their relationship in a
state-sanctioned fashion that provides full and equal recognition to all.

[
132
] This option does not seem to have been considered to date in
jurisdictions that have moved towards equal treatment for same-sex couples.
Nonetheless, in a discussion Paper released in December 2001, the Law
Commission of Canada has thrown open just such a possibility -- as well as
others -- for discussion. [See Note 26 below] Under the heading "Status
and Recognition" the Paper raises the following considerations for
discussion:

Clarifying legislative policies, avoiding
concepts like marriage and spouse wherever the policy or programme in question
does not relate to marriage, and developing new concepts that directly link the
policy being pursued to the observable facts of the relationships that
Parliament seeks to target can go a long way to ensuring the coherence, justice
and efficiency of the law.

Such a pragmatic approach does not, however,
address issues of symbolic status. This is why there is so much public debate
today about the recognition that the law now gives to one particular close
adult personal relationship

-- marriage. Many people claim that as long as Parliament continues to
recognize marriage as a privileged status relationship, all couples who wish to
marry should be permitted to do so.

. . . . .

Parliament has several options if it should
decide to reconsider the symbolic status that it affords to different close
adult personal relationships. First, it could redefine marriage to extend the
concept to other personal relationships that are excluded at present. Second,
it could supplement or replace the concept of marriage with a system of civil
registration of relationships. Third, it could establish a range of different
registered statuses so that people would be able to choose whatever status was
best suited to their particular relationship.

. . . . .

Redefining the concept of marriage

Many argue that Parliament should not hesitate to
define the term marriage to suit its own policy purposes. Presently, there is
one situation where there is a call for a secular definition of marriage that
departs significantly from most religious definitions -- the recognition of
same-sex marriages. Much of [page376] the opposition to expanding the
entitlement to marry in this manner comes from religious organizations, that
feel Parliament should not have the right to redefine a concept that, they
argue, was originally a religious one.

Others answer that while religious organizations
may continue to use the word marriage and limit how it is defined, they should
be allowed to do so only within their sphere, which is religious life.
Parliament should be entitled to define marriage however it likes for ordinary
legal purposes. Only in a theocracy, they observe, are secular concepts
necessarily identical to religious concepts.

It is therefore possible to imagine Parliament
establishing a civil, secular marriage in which same-sex or other relationships
are recognized, that would stand side-by-side with religious marriage as
defined by different sectarian authorities. Religions could continue to impose
their rules regarding eligibility for marriage, and marry only couples who
complied with those rules. This approach meets the status concerns of many
people who wish to get married but who cannot now do so.

The co-existence of civil marriage and domestic
partnership regimes may not, however, fully address the symbolic concerns of
those who now seek to have same-sex marriages recognized. As long as same-sex
couples are not entitled to marry, they argue, the registered domestic
partnership regime would just be giving them a second-class status. For this
reason, it may be that the registered domestic partnership regime is a viable
option for Parliament only if at the same time it both abolishes the concept of
civil marriage, and requires couples married in a religious ceremony to
register their status as domestic partners, just as they now must do to have
the marriage recognized by the state.

[
133
] Thus, there are other alternatives that might be weighed in
determining how marriage -- or the institution in present-day Canadian society
that will afford full and equal recognition to same-sex couples as marriage
presently does to opposite-sex couples -- is to be redefined, or reformulated.

[
134
] Even if opening up marriage to same-sex couples as the Dutch have done
[See Note 27 below] is the appropriate alternative, in order to comply with

Charter
dictates, legislatures and not courts are the proper venue for the
crafting of that solution, in my opinion. Even the Dutch "marriage"
maintains some distinctions between same-sex and opposite-sex marriages: [See
Note 28 below] same-sex marriage will have no consequences in relation to the
law of filiation based on descent, meaning that a child born into a same-sex
marriage will not have an automatic legal filiation link to both spouses;
presumptions of paternity do not apply; in the context of a marriage [page377]
between two men, a child born into the marriage by means of a surrogate mother
will have to be recognized by the biological father (or have paternity
judicially established), and be adopted by the other "parent" with
the consent of the mother; in the context of a marriage between two women, only
the biological mother would have a direct filiation link to the child and the
other parent would have to adopt; a Dutch same-sex marriage will not likely be
recognized abroad.

[
135
] Undoubtedly, issues similar to these will have to be addressed in
Canada, together possibly with other questions arising in connection with the
alternative birthing methods necessarily resorted to by same-sex couples. It
strikes me that such matters are more effectively dealt with by legislatures
rather than by the court simply "reformulating" the common law
definition of marriage by reading out the words "one man and one
woman" and reading in the words "two persons".

[
136
] For these reasons, I am satisfied the appropriate remedy in the
circumstances of this case is to strike down the common law definition, but to
suspend the operation of the declaration of invalidity for a period of time to
afford Parliament and the legislatures an opportunity to resolve the problem
before the declaration becomes effective. In the particular circumstances of
this case, I would also add a rider, or addendum, to the suspension.

[
137
] As I have noted at the outset of these reasons, the question raised in
these proceedings is deeply controversial in today's society. It touches the
core values and beliefs of Canadians across a broad cultural, political, moral
and religious spectrum in a profound way. It is a societal problem that is very
difficult to address and to resolve.

[
138
] The problem must be addressed and resolved, however, and this must be
done in a manner that accords to same-sex couples a recognition that is full
and equal to that enjoyed by opposite-sex couples. It is apparent on the record
before us that the process will be contentious, divisive, troublesome, and
potentially at risk of paralysis. What would be the consequences if the
legislative bodies were unable to craft a remedial solution and enact
legislation during the period of suspension, and the declaration of invalidity
-- with nothing more -- became effective? The legal framework for marriage, as
it presently exists -- governing a complex web of society's affairs -- would
disappear. What would be the implications of such a development for those who
are already married, their families and descendants, and those who are
contemplating marriage? The law must provide some element of stability and
certainty in people's lives. [page378]

[
139
] Nor do I think it is justified in the circumstances, to leave it to these
applicants, or others, to commence litigation and in effect start all over
again if Parliament (with the legislatures, where applicable) fails to create
appropriate remedial provisions in this area consistent with the requirements
of the
Charter
.

[
140
] For these reasons, I believe this to be a circumstance where an
addendum to the striking-down/suspension approach is appropriate. I therefore
conclude that, should Parliament (with the legislatures, where applicable)
decline to act within the prescribed time, the common law must be reformulated
in the fashion sought by the applicants. It should be clear, however, that if
such is the case, Parliament and the legislatures, by their inaction, have
chosen the route to be followed.

[
141
] I have had the opportunity to read the clear reasons of my colleague,
Associate Chief Justice Smith, who differs with me in this regard. We share the
strong conviction that it is the legislative branch of government which is best
equipped for the task of reformulating the common law definition of marriage,
and which has the primary responsibility for doing so. Respectfully, however, I
disagree with the Associate Chief Justice that the rider I propose to
incorporate into the remedy granted is too broad in the circumstances of this
case.

[
142
] To the contrary, I believe it is necessary to ensure that justice is
done in accordance with the
Charter
values and principles that govern Canadian
society today. I have no doubt the court has jurisdiction to make the order I
put forward. As Lamer C.J.C. observed, in Schachter v. Canada, supra, "a
court has flexibility in determining what course of action to take following a
violation of the Charter." Although the Chief Justice went on to refer to
the remedies of striking down, striking down with a temporary suspension (the
remedy selected by Smith A.C.J.S.C.), or reading down/reading in (the remedy
selected by LaForme J.), he went on to state that "in addition
s. 24
of
the Charter extends to any court . . . the power to grant an 'appropriate and
just' remedy to 'anyone whose [Charter] rights and freedoms . . . have been
infringed or denied'".

[
143
] Having regard to all of the circumstances, including the nature of the
violation of
Charter
principles here, the context of the specific legislation
that will require enactment, and the attendant conditions in which that
legislation must be crafted, I conclude that the appropriate disposition is (a)
to declare the common law definition of marriage constitutionally invalid, (b)
to suspend operation of the declaration of invalidity for 24 months to afford
Parliament (with the legislatures, where applicable) an opportunity to respond,
and (c) to declare that in the event Parliament (with the legislatures, where
applicable) does not enact [page379] legislation within that period, the common
law definition of marriage is to be reformulated as LaForme J. has ruled.

V. CONCLUSION AND DISPOSITION

[
144
] I have nothing further to add to the determination of LaForme J. with
respect to the argument based upon the division of powers under ss. 91 and 92
of the Constitution Act, and with respect to the
s. 2(a)
,
s. 2(b)
and
s. 7

Charter
arguments. I agree with him that they cannot succeed, in the
circumstances.

[
145
] For all of the foregoing reasons, then, I:

(a) declare the common law defining marriage as "the lawful and
voluntary union of one man and one woman to the exclusion of all others"
to be constitutionally invalid and inoperative;

(b) suspend the operation of the foregoing declaration for a period of 24
months to enable Parliament (and, where applicable, the legislatures) to bring
the law respecting marriage into line with the requirements of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms contained therein;

(c) but, should Parliament (and, where applicable, the legislatures) not act
accordingly prior to the expiration of 24 months, I declare in that event that
the common law definition of marriage -- that is, "the lawful and
voluntary union of one man and one woman to the exclusion of all others"
-- is to be reformulated by replacing the words "one man and one
woman" with the words "two persons".

[
146
] The applications are allowed in accordance with the foregoing
declarations. Should Parliament (and, where applicable, the legislatures) fail
to act, and option (c) above become effective, the applicants in each
application will be entitled to the orders in the nature of mandamus they seek.

[
147
] As the applicants have been substantially successful, the applicants
in both applications are entitled to their costs on a partial indemnity scale.
If the parties are unable to agree upon the amounts, the court may be spoken
to. There is an agreement, and an earlier decision made in these proceedings,
to the effect that none of the intervenors are entitled to claim or be awarded
costs.

[
148
] Order to go accordingly.

[1] LAFORME J.:-- The within applications that are the subject of this

examination into the historical societal institution of marriage. In direct
association with that, this court is called upon to examine the complex and
highly sensitive related issue of Canada's conceptions of equality and

[2] These proceedings considered two applications that were heard together.
The first requests that marriage licences be issued to permit same-sex couples

of Toronto (the "MCCT"), both as party intervenors.

[5] The respondents in this first application are the Attorney General of
Canada (the "AGC"), the Attorney General of Ontario (the

rule 13.01(1)
of the

of "marriage" in the

;

ss. 2
(a) (protected religious
freedoms) and 15(1) (equality rights) under the

and the breadth of any

PRELIMINARY ISSUES

[10] Before turning to the merits of the applications, I feel it is
important to briefly address two preliminary matters, namely, this court's
jurisdiction and the appropriate standard of review.

Jurisdiction

[11] At the outset, I wish to note that it would have been more appropriate,
and perhaps more practical, to pursue this issue in the first instance as an
ordinary application heard in the Superior Court. It is my understanding that
it proceeded in the Divisional Court more out of a desire expressed by the
applicants than by any procedural requirement. Nonetheless, I do not disagree
with the decision of Lang J. of August 29, 2000 wherein she decided that the
matter of the applicant Couples could be heard by the Divisional Court. [See
Note 31 below]

[12] As well, I do not disagree that it was proper, even if not more
expedient to join the application of the MCCT with that of the applicant
Couples and to hear both applications at the same time. [See Note 32 below]
Accordingly, I find that the matters are properly before this court upon the
same terms and conditions set out by Lang J. who was authorized to case manage
these matters up to the hearing. In my opinion, the correctness of Lang J.'s
decisions are supported by law and I believe it is necessary to touch upon that
in brief.

[13] Firstly, regarding the first application, the Divisional Court's authority
to hear an application for judicial review of a decision of the Clerk of the
City of Toronto is found in
s. 8
of the
Marriage Act
: [See Note 33 below]

. . . . .

(4) Review of refusal to issue licence -- Where
an issuer refuses to issue a licence, or the Minister refuses to issue an
authorization under subsection (3), the applicant may apply to the Divisional
Court for judicial review under the
Judicial Review Procedure Act
and for an
order directing that a licence [page383] be issued to the applicant and if the
court finds that the applicant is so entitled it may make such an order.

(5) Parties -- The applicant, the Minister and
such persons as the court may order are parties to an application under
subsection (4).

(6) Issue of licence under court order -- Where
an applicant for a licence files with an issuer, together with his or her
application, an order of the Divisional Court made on an application under
subsection (4) directing that a licence be issued to the applicant, the issuer
shall issue the licence.

(My emphasis)

[14] For purposes of this hearing, I find that when the City Clerk did not
issue the licence, but "held it in abeyance"; that was effectively
the same thing as a "refusal to issue a licence". The applicant
Couples could therefore properly apply to this court for a judicial review of
the Clerk's decision not to issue the licence.

[15] Further, there is the second application by the MCCT for judicial
review of the refusal of the Registrar General to register the marriage of two
same-sex couples. In connection with that refusal, the Registrar General's
statutory authority is set out in
ss. 19
and
20
of the
Vital Statistics Act
,
[See Note 34 below] which provide the following:

19(1) Every marriage that is solemnized in
Ontario shall be registered under this Act. R.S.O. 1980, c. 524, s. 15(1).

(2) If an officer designated under clause 60(m)
is satisfied as to the correctness and sufficiency of a statement of marriage
forwarded to the Registrar General under the regulations made under the

Marriage Act
, the officer shall register the marriage and upon request of the
person who solemnized the marriage, the officer shall mail an acknowledgment of
receipt of the statement of marriage to such person. R.S.O. 1980, c. 524, s.
15(2); 1981, c. 66, Sched.

20. If a marriage has not been registered within
one year from the day of the marriage, the registration may be made by the

R.S.O. 1980, c. 524, s. 16.

[16] Judicial review itself is a decision made in connection with the
exercise of a statutory power and, as a result, the Divisional Court has
jurisdiction to hear such applications. That authority for that principle is
found under
s. 6(1)
of the
Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. J.1
,
which provides that:

6(1) Subject to subsection (2), an application
for judicial review shall be made to the Divisional Court.

[17] Finally, and in addition,
s. 2(1)
of the
Judicial Review Procedure Act

states that:

2(1) On an application by way of originating
notice, which may be styled "Notice of Application for Judicial
Review", the court may, despite any right [page384] of appeal, by order
grant any relief that the applicant would be entitled to in any one or more of
the following:

1. Proceedings by way of application for an
order in the nature of mandamus, prohibition, or certiorari.

. . . . .

[18] Therefore, and as I noted above, consistent with the decisions of Lang
J., I am satisfied that both of the within applications are properly before
this court for hearing.

Standard of Review

[19] All participants to these proceedings proceeded on the basis that it
was unnecessary to address the question of the applicable standard of review. Indeed,
the court did not request submissions on this issue. Nonetheless, although the
issue of the applicable standard of review for each of the within applications
was not the subject of submissions at the hearing, I believe I should briefly
address it, if only to better complete the record.

[20] I find that the appropriate standard of review for the decision of the
City Clerk to hold a marriage licence in abeyance and the Registrar General's
refusal to issue a marriage licence following the publication of the banns is,
in each case, "correctness". I reach this decision by applying a
"pragmatic and functional approach", [which] was mandated by the
Supreme Court of Canada in Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and
Immigration). [See Note 35 below]

[21] In Baker, the court held that one factor to be considered in assessing
the correctness of an administrative decision is the presence or absence of a
privative clause. And, on that point, there is no privative clause to insulate
the decisions made in the within case under the
Vital Statistics Act
, or the

Marriage Act
, from the court's scrutiny.

[22] Another factor I considered in deciding if the standard of review is
"correctness", and one that was also mentioned in Baker, is whether
the decisions before this court are determinations of questions of pure law. In
that regard, both the Registrar General and the City Clerk considered whether
the respective parties involved had the capacity to marry. They made their
decisions, at least in part, on the basis that this was a matter of federal
jurisdiction. That in itself is a live issue and is a question of general law.
[page385]

[23] Finally, the applicants together assert that the actions of the City
Clerk and the Registrar General infringe their constitutional rights as
guaranteed by the
Charter of Rights
and Freedoms. Obviously, if this court
finds that the actions of either the City Clerk or the Registrar General are
unconstitutional, then their actions would be subject to demanding scrutiny,
and if found to be wanting, may be set aside.

[24] In all respects, and relying on the reasons just stated above, I find
that the standard of "correctness" must be applied to the
interpretations of the
Marriage Act
and the
Vital Statistics Act
by the City
Clerk and the Registrar General.

THE ISSUES

[25] The core of virtually all of the issues that are for consideration by
this court are found in the position advanced by the applicant Couples. In my
view, their stated position, or their indictment, underlies the arguments of
all the other participants and any contrary positions advanced are directed to
the fundamental charges and propositions proffered by the applicant Couples.

[26] In very general terms, the applicant Couples submit that their right of
grievance is because excluding gays and lesbians from marriage denies them one
of the most fundamental of all human and civil rights in Canada. They argue
that freedom to marry is so central to Canada's definition of humanity that a
marriage ban against an entire class of people unavoidably implicates numerous

Charter
rights and freedoms.

[27] The applicant Couples further submit that their exclusion from marriage
offends human dignity by withholding the rights of equality, liberty and
security, and it infringes the freedoms of expression, conscience and
association on the basis of sex. They argue further still that there is no
pressing and substantial objective in denying lesbians and gay men the freedom
to marry their chosen partners. Indeed, they say the contrary is in fact the
case. That is, they say that the recognition of the marriages of same-sex
spouses would in fact accord with the laudatory purposes of marriage
recognition.

[28] However, before setting out what I view as being the fundamental
questions for this court to answer in order to decide the applications before
it, I believe it will be useful to outline -- in some detail -- the positions
of the parties. In my opinion, this is necessary given that this case is of
significant importance to all the parties who participated and presented
argument before this court. Indeed, I would expect that the questions posed,
the [page386] submissions made and the answers by this court are equally
important to most all Canadians.

[29] Therefore, because of its significance, I believe it will be both
informative and fair to all those interested and concerned to supply the
respective positions of the parties in some detail. In that regard, I have set
out below the sum and substance of the positions of each of the parties who
argued before this court. I have attempted to do so in a somewhat summary form
and trust that because of that I have not misinterpreted or misstated their
positions.

Applicant Couples

[30] The applicant Couples submit that same-sex couples must be free to
marry since any exclusion of gays, lesbians and bisexuals from this fundamental
social institution is unconstitutional. They say that this is even more the
case because they are already a disadvantaged group. With that as the
foundation, the applicant Couples submit that the following are the issues for
the court to consider and that are determinative of this case:

(i) There is no statutory impediment to the
issuance of marriage licences to same-sex couples who otherwise meet the
requisite criteria. The capacity to marry is within federal jurisdiction under

s. 92(12)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
.

(ii) There is no common law rule preventing the
issuance of marriage licences. Even if there were a bar to marriage between persons
of the same sex at common law, this court may reformulate the law to conform
with
Charter
values.

(iii) Any common law rule denying equal marriage would be unconstitutional

THE CORE OF THE RELEVANT LAW

[51] Much of the state of the law that has evolved and that is directly on
the issue of marriage is not really contested. But, what is in serious dispute
is whether or not the basic understandings that exist from that law are either
sound, or whether they remain sound. For purposes of my analysis -- and
reflecting my comprehension of the state of the law -- I propose to set out
some of those basic legal understandings.

[52] The law that I intend to review briefly under this heading is limited
to Canadian jurisprudence. There are of course other directly related judicial
authorities from other countries that are relied upon by the parties herein.
This court was referred to court decisions that included the jurisdictions of
Great Britain, New Zealand and the United States. And while it is unnecessary
to review them at this time, I will have occasion to consider and comment on
some of them later on in these reasons.

Regarding Marriage

[53] The authority to define marriage is found under the head of power set
out in s. 91(26) of the Constitution Act and is, therefore, under federal
jurisdiction. Specifically, this head of [page394] power authorizes the
Parliament of Canada to make laws for "Marriage and Divorce". [See
Note 36 below] To date, the only statutory pronouncement that can be said to
amount to a definition of marriage in the exercise of this head of federal
power is found in the recent
Modernization of Benefits and Obligations Act

("MBOA"). [See Note 37 below]

[54] The
MBOA
amended 68 federal statutes to include same-sex spouses in the
definition of "common-law partners". This statute was the federal
Parliament's response to the Supreme Court of Canada decision of M. v. H. that
found
s. 29
of the
Family Law Act of Ontario
to be discriminatory because it
excluded same-sex partners from spousal support obligations and benefits. [See
Note 38 below] The MBOA grants unmarried different and same-sex
"common-law partners" almost all the same rights and obligations as
married spouses in federal law.

[55] The only specific provisions of the
MBOA
that are relevant to the
within applications are found in the interpretation clause [at s. 1.1]. That
clause provides that:

1.1 For greater certainty, the amendments made by
this Act do not affect the meaning of the word "marriage", that is,
the lawful union of one man and one woman to the exclusion of all others. [See
Note 39 below]

[56] The actual legal definition of marriage is said to have its roots in
the common law and the statutory marriage laws of England. It is generally
understood that at common law the definition that is routinely referred to is
found in the statement of Lord Penzance in the 1866 English case of Hyde v.
Hyde and Woodmansee. That definitional statement is said to be, "the
voluntary union for life of one man and one woman, to the exclusion of all
others". And, because it will be a continuous point of reference throughout
these reasons, the entire statement of Lord Penzance is as follows:

I conceive that marriage, as understood in
Christendom, may for this purpose be defined as the voluntary union for life of
one man and one woman, to the exclusion of all others. [See Note 40 below]

Layland v. Ontario

[57] In 1993, this Divisional Court had occasion to consider the issue of
marriage and it was generally within the same context as [page395] the within
applications. The case is Layland v. Ontario (Minister of Consumer and
Commercial Relations) and is one in which the majority of the court, and
relying on English authority including Hyde v. Hyde, found that:

. . . under the common law of Canada applicable
to Ontario a valid marriage can take place only between a man and a woman, and
that persons of the same sex do not have the capacity to marry one another.
[See Note 41 below]

[58] However, to complete the judicial pronouncement, Greer J. offered a
dissenting opinion and held that:

. . . restricting marriages to heterosexual
couples infringes and violates the applicants'
s. 15(1)

Charter
rights and that
such violation cannot be justified under
s. 1
of the Charter. I also agree . .
. that there is no common law prohibition against same-sex marriages in Canada.
[See Note 42 below]

[59] While federal Parliament has legislative authority to define marriage
and, therefore, who has the capacity to marry, the provinces have jurisdiction
over the "Solemnization of Marriage in the Province" pursuant to
s.
92(12)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
. In Ontario, this is exercised through the

Marriage Act
, which basically governs how people get married. For example, it
provides that no marriage is solemnized without a valid licence issued pursuant
to the Act or the "publication of banns". [See Note 43 below] The
Marriage Act goes on [in
s. 5
] to prescribe certain limits on who can be
married, and this is described as being:

5(1) Any person who is of the age of majority may
obtain a licence or be married under the authority of the publication of banns,
provided no lawful cause exists to hinder the solemnization. [See Note 44
below]

(My emphasis)

[60] Although marriage itself is not defined in the
Marriage Act, s. 24(3)

states that during the marriage ceremony the persons being married are required
to be declared "husband and wife". Further in this regard, the
marriage licence application authorized by the regulations passed pursuant to
the
Marriage Act
refers to a "bride" and "bridegroom". [See
Note 45 below]

[61] Generally speaking, the term "lawful cause" [which] is used
in the
Marriage Act
and referenced above, [and] can be a [page396] bar to a
marriage, instituted either at common law or by legislation, includes (i) a
prior existing marriage; (ii) being underage; (iii) prohibited degrees (i.e.
brother and sister); and (iv) mental disability or illness.

[62] As for the publication of banns: that refers to a public notice given
in a place of worship that a marriage between two people is to take place. This
is intended to give the congregation the opportunity to express their knowledge
of any impediment to the marriage. It is a traditional method of solemnizing a
marriage, which has been practised for many years within some religious
denominations. [See Note 46 below]

[63] In addition to the above-noted Ontario case of Layland -- and before
leaving this area of overview -- I believe it will be helpful to outline two
other relevant Canadian judicial pronouncements that involved the issue of
same-sex marriage. Both are trial court decisions and each specifically address
the sum and substance of the issues that are squarely before this court.

Re North and Matheson

[64] In Re North and Matheson, [See Note 47 below] an application was brought
under
s. 35(1)
of the
Vital Statistics Act
[See Note 48 below] of Manitoba for
an order requiring the acceptance of an application to register the marriage of
the applicants. The same-sex applicants had completed a marriage ceremony and
sought to register their marriage arguing that they had complied with all the
requirements of the
Marriage Act
. [See Note 49 below] The application was
refused.

[65] Relying almost exclusively on those judicial authorities that addressed
the division of powers under the
Constitution Act, 1867
, the court in Matheson
found that: (i) provinces have the exclusive power to make laws regarding the
solemnization of marriage, and (ii) the federal Parliament has not legislated
that the union between two males is not a marriage. In addition, the court
further found that the Province of Manitoba had not legislated that such a
marriage cannot be solemnized.

[66] In spite of the absence of any specific legislative prohibition, the
court nonetheless decided to dismiss the application. [page397] The
justification for the dismissal was generally founded on the language of
s. 2

of the
Marriage Act
. It provides that:

2. If duly authorized as herein provided, a
person eighteen years of age or more who is,

(i) a minister, a clergyman, a rabbi, or an
official of a religious denomination corresponding to a minister, clergyman, or
a rabbi, duly ordained or appointed according to the rites and ceremonies of
the religious denomination to which he belongs; or

(ii) a catechist, an evangelist, a missionary, or
a theological student duly appointed or commissioned by the governing body of a
religious denomination with special authority to solemnize marriages;

may solemnize the ceremony of marriage between
any two persons not under a legal disqualification to contract the marriage.

(My emphasis)

[67] The decision turned on the interpretation to be given to the phrase
"any two persons". The court rejected the argument that the
legislature -- in using the words "any two persons" -- intended to
recognize the capacity of two persons of the same sex to marry. Moreover, even
if such an argument were accepted, the court held that such matters relate to
capacity to marry and, as such, was ultra vires the province given that
capacity was a matter completely within the competence of the Parliament of
Canada. [See Note 50 below]

[68] Finally, on the issue of capacity to marry, the court found this to be
a matter of common law and in that regard relied on the definition that is said
to flow from Hyde v. Hyde. [See Note 51 below] The court's reasons included the
finding that the sex of the participants in a marriage is clearly an essential
component of the relationship called marriage because it has always been
recognized as the union of one man and one woman. As a result, the application
was refused because, unless a marriage involves one man and one woman, there
can be no marriage. In the opinion of the court, there was nothing to be
registered:

That the applicants purported to comply with all
the conditions of solemnization prescribed in the
Marriage Act
cannot alter the
fact that a marriage did not take place. [See Note 52 below]

EGALE v. AGBC

[69] On October 2, 2001, Pittfield J. of the B.C. Supreme Court released
reasons in the case of EGALE v. AGC in connection with [page398] an action that
was virtually identical to that of the case at bar. Indeed -- other than the
MCCT -- the parties who presented argument before Pittfield J. were, on the
whole, the same as those who appeared and argued before this court. [See Note
53 below]

[70] Briefly, in EGALE, Pittfield J. dismissed the multiple applications
that had sought a declaration that marriage of same-sex partners is not
prohibited at common law, or that to deny such marriages infringed the rights,
protections and guarantees of [the]
Charter
. More specifically, Pittfield J.
dismissed the applications and found that:

(i) The common law governing the question of
capacity to marry did not recognize the marriage of two persons of the same
sex; and

(ii) Because the capacity to marry was exclusively within federal
constitutional jurisdiction, only the federal government could enact
legislation to redefine marriage or change the rules on capacity.

[71] Once again, because of the similarities in the case at bar and that
argued in EGALE, I believe it will be useful and informative to set out a more
particularized -- although somewhat condensed -- account of the reasons for the
decision of Pittfield J. In sum, his reasons and some of his findings include:

1. The common-law definition of marriage is ".
. . a lawful and monogamous union of two persons of opposite sex".

2. That to change the common-law rule, a court must
do it "incrementally". In that regard, granting the change requested
in the common law would affect a "deep-rooted and social
institution". Some examples cited include:

consummated marriages require "heterosexual intercourse", and a
ground of divorce is adultery. Thus, a change in the common law rule requires
too many affected changes. Parties need to know before entering into marriage
"what factors

(if any) may result in a marriage being void, voidable, or subject to
dissolution".

3. Regarding s. 91(26) (Marriage and Divorce) and
s. 92(13)

(Property and Civil Rights) of the
Constitution Act, 1867
, he held: Marriage in
1867 unambiguously meant a "monogamous [page399] opposite-sex
relationship". Therefore, any attempt to change this meaning would amount
to a unilateral amendment to the constitution. "The requirement that
parties to a legal marriage be of opposite sex goes to the core of the
relationship and has nothing to do with capacity." Thus, federal
Parliament cannot amend the meaning of marriage. Moreover, solemnization of
same- sex marriages cannot fall within provincial authority because the only
valid marriage is an opposite-sex marriage. Specifically Pittfield J. held
that:

-- Since "marriage" in the constitution
is defined as opposite-sex couples, any amendment to the definition requires
the formal constitutional amendment process. Furthermore, the
Charter
cannot be
used to invalidate another constitutional provision.

[72] However, in spite of his just noted decisions, Pittfield J. then went
on to consider those arguments advanced to support the various
Charter

challenges. Once again, he decided that the applicants could not succeed and
the applications were dismissed. In that regard, he concluded that, if the
Charter were to apply, then the issues should be decided as follows:

-- Section 2(b) "Freedom of Expression":
this merely guarantees the freedom to express thoughts or opinions made either
orally or in writing. It does not include the expressing of love and commitment
to a chosen partner through marriage.

-- Section 2(d) "Freedom of Association":
this guarantee is directed at assemblies and associations that go beyond the
intimate circle of family. Denying same-sex marriage is not a denial of the
freedom of association.

-- Section 6 "mobility": this is intended
to ensure that provinces do not apply different standards to newly arrived
residents as opposed to the population of the province as a whole. There is no
suggestion that same-sex couples who move from one province to another are
treated differently from the general population of the province.

-- Section 7 "Liberty and Security of
Person": the restricted definition of marriage does not deny anyone's
capacity to live together in any kind of arrangement and on whatever terms they
choose. The law of marriage does not interfere with bodily integrity, nor does
it impose psychological stress that would amount to an infringement of security
of the person. [page400]

-- Section 15 -- "Equality": same-sex
couples do not have the same choice available to them as opposite-sex couples
because of their sexual orientation and for that reason only they cannot obtain
a marriage licence. That amounts to a denial of an equal benefit of the law and
is a violation of
s. 15
. The distinction of sexual orientation is an
"analogous ground" and the discrimination is substantive. Contextually,
the law omitting same-sex couples enhances the stereotypical view that same-sex
relationships are less important or valuable than opposite- sex relationships.
Accordingly, s. 15 is violated. However, under s. 1, the objective of
preserving the original constitutional intention of marriage (i.e.
opposite-sex) is "pressing and substantial". The opposite- sex
requirement is the primary means by which humankind perpetuates itself in our
society. Thus there is requisite proportionality between the equality violation
and the purpose for it.

[73] In the end, Pittfield J. was of the opinion that all of the
Charter

analysis was unnecessary because marriage is a constitutionally defined term.
And -- as I noted above -- he held that any attempts to redefine the term
through legislation would amount to a unilateral attempt to amend the
constitution. As well, he held that marriage is also a defined term at common
law and those changes sought by the applicants amounted to changes to the
common law that are more than incremental.

[74] As for any remedy -- given his dismissal of the applications --
Pittfield J. was not required to offer any opinion on this issue. However, he
was of the view that the applicants' concerns could be achieved through
provinces choosing and legislating other forms of recognition and formalization
of same-sex relationships.

[75] In connection with this last point taken from EGALE, other provinces
have indeed legislated regimes for same-sex couples that are supposed to
parallel marriage. Furthermore, recent decisions of the Supreme Court have also
caused legislative action both at the federal and provincial levels that are
supposed to address issues of same-sex relationships. For reference purposes --
and because it is offered as being an answer to the concerns of the applicants
-- I have briefed some of that activity below.

Regarding Same-Sex Rights

[76] Marriage aside, in Ontario some same-sex spousal rights have been
granted. For example, the Supreme Court of Canada [page401] case of M. v. H.
[See Note 54 below] resulted in legislation being amended to provide that gay
and lesbian couples are to be treated on an equal basis with heterosexual
couples. However, it is to be noted that at the time of the passing of this
legislation the Ontario government was clear:

the definitions of "spouse" and "marital status" were not
being changed. The then-Attorney-General explained the Ontario government's
position as follows:

Marriage is not affected by this bill. There are
certain unique rights and responsibilities that relate to marriage that are not
affected by this bill. . . . Marriage, as members know, involves a man and a
woman in Ontario . . . I stress that this bill reserves the definition of
"spouse" and "marital status" for a man and a woman, the
traditional definition of "family" in Ontario. The bill introduces
into law a new term called "same-sex partner", while at the same time
protecting the traditional definitions of "spouse" and "marital
status". [See Note 55 below]

[77] In the province of Quebec, marriage is controlled by the
Quebec Civil
Code
, which at least until recently, explicitly prohibited same-sex marriages.
Article 365 of the Code provided that "[m]arriage may be contracted only
between a man and a woman expressing openly their free and enlightened
consent." Until recently, the written law pertaining to capacity
("conditions de fond du marriage") in Quebec was found in provisions
of the pre-confederation Civil Code of Lower Canada (CCLC). [See Note 56 below]

[78] On May 7, 2001, the federal Parliament adopted Bill S-4, the Federal
Law -- Civil Harmonization Act. Part I of that Act contains various provisions
on capacity to marry that apply in Quebec, including an express statement that
marriage is between man and a woman. [See Note 57 below]

[79] Quebec legislation in 1999 amended 28 administrative laws and 11
regulations to grant same-sex couples the same benefits and obligations already
available to opposite-sex couples; however it was apparently not the intention
of the legislation to reform the Civil Code. The legislation amended statutes
[page402] and regulations that contained a definition of the concept of
"de facto spouse" (conjoint de fait) to allow de facto unions to be
recognized without regard to the sex of the persons concerned. The affect of
the legislation was in connection with areas of the law such as workplace
