compensation and labour standards, pension statutes, public sector retirement
benefits and some social assistance legislation.

[80] However, even more recently, on December 7, 2001, the Quebec government
introduced a draft of Bill 84. This Bill recognizes civil unions for gay and
lesbian couples. The legislation changes
Quebec's Civil Code
to create a new
status of partners, allowing same-sex couples to enter into a civil union with
rights similar to those of married couples. In its original form, this Bill did
not allow same-sex couples to adopt children.

[81] Bill 84 gives same-sex couples most of the legal benefits of marriage,
including division of assets after a breakup, the right to see a partner's
medical records and automatic status as a beneficiary when a partner dies. In
addition, inheritance rights as well as those pertaining to pensions and health
insurance are to be extended to same-sex couples. Moreover, same-sex civil
unions would also include the rights that have been granted to same-sex couples
since 1999.

[82] In early June of 2002, the National Assembly of Quebec adopted Bill 84.
In addition to the elements of the draft bill described above, Bill 84 also extended
full parental rights to same-sex couples in Quebec. In this respect, for the
first time in Canada, gay and lesbian couples will be legally recognized as the
legitimate parents of the children they raised. Ultimately, both partners in a
civil union will have a legal responsibility in the upbringing of any children
and will both be financially obligated to the children in the case of divorce.
Similar legislation, with respect to the adoption of children by same-sex
partners, has recently also been introduced in the Province of Manitoba.

[83] Bill 84 makes Quebec the second Canadian province, after Nova Scotia,
to recognize civil unions for gay and lesbian couples. Of note is the fact that
the minister responsible in Quebec expressed the view that the federal
government should consider similar changes to make federal laws compatible with
Quebec's proposals.

[84] In 2001, Manitoba enacted omnibus legislation under the Act to Comply
with the Supreme Court of Canada Decision in M. v. H. [See Note 58 below] This
legislation amended several Manitoba statutes [page403] and extended spousal
rights and responsibilities to cohabiting same-sex couples in areas such as
superannuation, dependant's relief, family maintenance, survivor's benefits,
pension benefits and workers' compensation benefits.

[85] In 2000, Nova Scotia passed legislation that is, on the whole, similar
to the legislative changes in other provincial jurisdictions in Canada. The
legislation formulates a domestic partner registry and grants domestic partners
generally the same rights and obligations as spouses. A unique feature in Nova
Scotia is that it creates and defines a "domestic partner".
Section
52
(a) of the
Vital Statistics Act
[See Note 59 below] provides that a
"domestic partner" means:

. . . an individual who is a party to a
registered domestic- partner declaration made in accordance with Section 53 and
does not include former domestic partner;

[86] While several other European countries recognize a system of same-sex
registered partnerships; the Netherlands formally recognizes marriage as
including a union of two persons of the same sex. As of April 1, 2001, through
legislation, marriage in the Netherlands has been extended to include same-sex
couples. To my knowledge, the Netherlands is the only jurisdiction that
recognizes same-sex marriages.

[87] It is my intention that, by providing the above statements of the
positions of the parties, a brief account of some of the relevant law and some
of the related government action as background, the essence of the within
applications will be given a clearer perspective. That foundational background,
submit the applicants, is what gives testament to, and demonstrates, the
totality of their unconstitutional exclusion from the fundamental institution
of marriage. I turn now to my analysis of the issues and my decision as to
whether or not the applicants are correct.

ANALYSIS

[88] As I noted above, I intend to decide these applications by examining
the issues and answering the specific statement of issues as posed by the
applicant Couples. And again, where appropriate, I will address the submissions
and arguments made by the respondents and the various intervenors within my
analysis of the applicant Couples' statement of issues. Turning then to the
first issue. [page404]

(i) Is There a Statutory Impediment to the Issuance of Marriage Licences to
Same-Sex Couples?

[89] In the context of the within applications, there can be no question that
the exclusive authority to legislate "capacity" to marry rests
exclusively with the federal Parliament pursuant to
s. 91(26)
of the

Constitution Act, 1867
. It is equally clear that the extent of provincial
jurisdiction in connection with marriage is limited to the
"solemnization" or celebration of marriage as authorized by
s.
92(12)
. The foundation of the within applications speaks to the issue of
"capacity" to marry, or, the sex of those persons who seek to marry
one another.

[90] The first, and perhaps obvious, thing that can be said on this issue is
that there is no lawful impediment that is specific to sex, statutory or
otherwise, that prevents gays and lesbians from marrying, provided they marry
someone of the opposite sex. [See Note 60 below] However -- as is perhaps
equally obvious -- the real question to be decided under this issue is whether
or not there exists any statute that provides an impediment for same-sex
marriages.

[91] There are, as briefly noted above, some expressions in the
Marriage Act

of Ontario and the regulations thereto that appear to at least infer that
marriages are considered to be between men and women. For example, s. 24(3) of
that Act specifies that persons being married are to be declared "husband
and wife", and there is the reference in the Regulations to the Act to a
"bride" and a "bridegroom". [See Note 61 below]

[92] However, as the
Marriage Act
is provincial legislation, whatever its
intention may be, it has no binding legal impact on this specific issue. To
interpret the references as having an intention other than an attempt to
reflect the state of the law as it is believed to be by Ontario would be to
give effect to a law that is ultra vires the province. [See Note 62 below]
Thus, any such pronouncements in provincial legislation as to capacity can only
be interpreted as an expression of the view as to what the federal state of the
law is. By themselves, the provincial legislative pronouncements as to capacity
are not binding.

[93] As for federal legislation, generally speaking, it has never expressly
legislated capacity to marry in relation to the sex of the respective parties.
The only federal legislation that [page405] makes an express reference to
capacity is found [in] the
Marriage (Prohibited Degrees) Act
, which forbids
persons from marrying if they are related to each other within certain
prohibited degrees of consanguinity. [See Note 63 below]

[94] Indeed -- and as I previously noted -- the only federal statutory
pronouncement on the capacity to marry based upon gender is found in the
MBOA
.
And again, that is found in the "interpretation" clause at s. 1.1 and
states that the meaning of "marriage" is unaffected by the passage of
the Act. However, it goes on to provide that "marriage", as
referenced in the section, means "the lawful union of one man and one
woman to the exclusion of all others."

[95] In my opinion, it is significant to the within issues that the
MBOA
was
not a statute passed by Parliament that is directed at marriage but rather, it
is specific to "same-sex common law couples". The Act is clearly not
intended to define marriage and I would say it goes to some lengths to affirm
this fact.

[96] In addition to
s. 1.1
-- which is merely a guide to the interpretation
of the statute -- the government has also published a "backgrounder"
document that emphasizes yet again that the definition of marriage is not to be
changed by the
MBOA
. [See Note 64 below] In the end, it simply cannot be said
that the MBOA amounts to legislation that the federal Parliament ever intended
to be in relation to marriage. Following this analysis, it would seem equally
clear that it cannot be interpreted as legislation that Parliament intended
should act as an impediment to the marriage of persons of the same sex.

[97] I can agree with the submissions of the AGC, on the point that
Parliament's concerns and intentions with respect to the definition of marriage
were expressed before, during and after the passage of the
MBOA
. However, I do
not agree that the Act itself can in any way be said to define an aspect of
capacity to marry. I will, however, permit that one must accept that the
circumscribed pronouncements of Parliament contained in the MBOA do provide
insight into what Parliament believes the definition of marriage to be. That
is, it seems clear that it generally believes that marriage means the union of
"one man and one woman to the exclusion of all others".

[98] Before continuing on, this seems an opportune time to address an issue
primarily advanced by the intervenor, the [page406] Association. It submits
that this court does not possess the jurisdiction to grant the relief sought by
the applicants.

[99] The submission of the Association on this court's lack of jurisdiction
is founded in the language of the
Constitution Act, 1867
. Specifically, it
argues that ss. 91(26) and 92(12) of the Constitution Act -- when using the
word "marriage" -- contain within that word a clear, constitutionally
enshrined meaning: "the union between a man and a woman". The
argument then goes on to assert that, therefore, any change to the meaning of
the word "marriage" found in ss. 91 and 92 requires a formal
amendment to the Constitution Act.

[100] Simply put, the Association argues that the meaning of the word
"marriage" contained in the Constitution Act, expressly limits
Parliament to legislating under that head of power to unions between one man
and one woman. It goes on to say that the power granted to Parliament under
that head of legislative authority does not authorize it to legislate with
respect to unions between members of the same sex. Similarly, under
s. 92(12)
,
a province can only solemnize marriages between a man and a woman; a province
does not possess the constitutional power to solemnize "marriages"
between members of the same sex.

[101] In sum, the Association submits that the impediment to the applicants'
claim for the legal recognition of marriage between same-sex couples does not
lie in federal or provincial legislation -- or in the common law -- but rather
in the language of the Constitution itself. Respectfully, I disagree.

[102] In my opinion, the Association's submission in this regard amounts to
an attempt to freeze a meaning that may have been understood by the framers of
the Constitution back in 1867. Such a proposition is unsupportable in law.

[103] At the outset such a proposition contravenes the basic principle of
Canadian constitutional interpretation that "the B.N.A. Act planted in
Canada a living tree capable of growth and expansion within its natural limits."
[See Note 65 below]

[104] I am very mindful that Pittfield J. in EGALE reached an opposite
conclusion on this issue than I have. In his reasons for his decision, and
after a thorough and thoughtful examination of the issue and some of the
related law, he held that:

The relief sought, namely the characterization of
same-sex relationships as marriages, cannot be delivered by Parliament under s.
91(26) of the [page407] Constitution of Canada without an amendment to the
Constitution procured with the agreement of the provinces in the manner
contemplated by the
Constitution Act, 1982
. [See Note 66 below]

[105] In my analysis, I would begin by restating the trite principle that s.
91 grants Parliament exclusive jurisdiction "to make laws" over a
list of matters or subjects. Section 91(26) -- "Marriage and Divorce"
-- merely sets out a head of power and there is no definition to either term,
although in 1867 there no doubt was an understanding of what the word meant.
The purpose of
s. 91
was not to entrench a particular set of rules, but rather
it was to confer jurisdiction to make rules, including the jurisdiction to fix
the qualifying factors for and incidents of the status of marriage.

[106] Given that "marriage" refers only to a topic or "class
of subjects" [See Note 67 below] of potential legislation, it cannot
contain an internal frozen-in-time meaning that reflects the presumed framers'
intent as it may have been in 1867. It must -- as the authorities have
proclaimed -- be interpreted "as describing a subject for legislation, not
a definite object". Canadian courts have repeatedly declared that the
language of the B.N.A. Act "must be given a large and liberal
interpretation" recognizing "the magnitude of the subject with which
it purports to deal in very few words". [See Note 68 below]

[107] By way of what I believe is an apt example,
s. 91(24)
of the

Constitution Act, 1867
sets out a federal head of exclusive jurisdiction as
being: "Indians, and Lands reserved for the Indians". When presented
with this same example, Pittfield J. decided that:

In the course of argument, it was suggested that
the
Indian Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I.5
, provides support [for] the proposition
that Parliament can define a head of power. The argument is that in accordance
with the exclusive authority conferred by
s. 91(24)
of the
Constitution Act,
1867
with respect to "Indians, and lands reserved for the Indians",
Parliament enacted the Indian Act that defines "Indian" to mean
"a person who pursuant to this Act is registered as an Indian or is
entitled to be registered as an Indian", thereby suggesting that those who
do not meet the criteria are not Indians.

I am not persuaded by the argument. The Supreme
Court of Canada has ruled that the reference to "Indian" in
s. 91(24)

is a reference to the aboriginal peoples of Canada. If an individual is
aboriginal, the character cannot be taken away by registration or entitlement
to register. The definition in the
Indian Act
does nothing more than ensure
that, of all persons who are [page408] Indian, only those who register or are
entitled to register will be entitled to the benefits or obligations imposed by
the Act. That is far different from attempting to define who is or is not
"Indian" or what is or is not marriage. [See Note 69 below]

[108] Respectfully, it is my opinion that Pittfield J. was incorrect in his
analysis. In particular, I believe he was wrong when he found that the
Indian
Act
does nothing more than ensure that those persons "who are Indian"
are entitled to be registered under the Act. The consequence of the Indian Act,
particularly when defining "Indian", does far more than that. In what
follows is my attempt to illustrate why.

[109] Prior to 1985, the
Indian Act
provided -- perhaps incredulously by
today's understandings -- that a non-Indian or non-Aboriginal woman could marry
an Indian man and by that act she would become an Indian. [See Note 70 below]
Such a result amounts to much more than ensuring that "those persons who
are Indians" may be registered to receive the benefits and obligations
imposed by the Act.

[110] Aboriginal people as defined by
s. 35(2)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982

includes "Indians". [See Note 71 below] That must obviously in turn
include those non-Aboriginal Indians who otherwise qualified and were registered
under that prior
Indian Act
. Indeed, the definition of Indian was amended yet
again in the Indian Act in 1985: after the incorporation of the Charter of
Rights and Freedoms into our Constitution. The elementary point of this
illustration is simply: the class of persons (i.e. "Indians") under

s. 91(24)
can, and has been changed by Parliament many times since the time of
Confederation.

[111] The illustration is intended to show that, while the definition of
Indian in the
Indian Act
is at times different than it is in the
Constitution
Act, 1982
; Indian in the constitution always includes Indian as defined by the
Indian Act. And although the two definitions are not always the same -- nor do
they have to be -- they obviously can be. That is, federal Parliament is not
limited to legislating in strict compliance with a definition of a term that
may have been originally understood in a legislative head of jurisdiction.

[112] To my mind, it is a simple proposition. If Parliament can legislate
the capacity to be an Indian that is different from the [page409] definition
that may have been understood at the time of Confederation, [See Note 72 below]
then it must also be able to legislate the capacity to enter into marriage
beyond that which may also have been understood at the time.

[113] A further submission in connection with this issue relates to the
Association's reliance on the interpretive analysis undertaken in the case of
Re Eskimo. [See Note 73 below] It submits that the same analysis as applied in
that case should be followed in deciding the within applications. Once again, I
must respectfully disagree.

[114] In 1939, in the case of Re Eskimo, the Supreme Court was concerned
with a controversy that had arisen between the then-Dominion Government and the
Government of Quebec over legislative jurisdiction over the Eskimo (Inuit)
inhabitants of Quebec. The issue for the court was to decide whether the term
"Indian" as used in the constitutional head of power, "Indians
and Lands Reserved for the Indians" included the Aboriginal peoples then
referred to as Eskimos. The analysis followed by the court was to examine the
definition of "Indian" as it was understood at the time of
Confederation.

[115] In my opinion, the type of analysis used in Re Eskimo is limited to
the specific facts and unique issues of the case. At the risk of
oversimplifying the principle, it applies in the instance where the levels of
government each assert legislative authority over the "subject matter"
(i.e. "Indians"). It is not an appropriate analysis where -- as in
the case at bar -- the levels of government agree that the subject matter,
namely marriage, is properly within federal jurisdiction.

[116] I agree with the MCCT that the more appropriate and adopted
"progressive approach" to constitutional interpretation should be
followed and applied to the within case. Such an approach is intended to allow
for the constitution to change with the needs and values of society. That
approach is most appropriate in all the circumstances of, and especially given
the nature of the issues underlying, the within applications.

[117] In addition, I believe that because the
Charter
is part of the
constitution, that Charter must be brought to bear and applied in any judicial
interpretation of s. 91(26). In that way, applying a progressive approach
allows a constitution to endure and avoid obsolescence as society evolves. As
was judiciously noted in Hunter v. Southam Inc.: [page410]

A statute defines present rights and obligations.
It is easily enacted and as easily repealed. A constitution, by contrast, is
drafted with an eye to the future. Its function is to provide a continuing
framework for the legitimate exercise of governmental power and, when joined by
a Bill or a
Charter of Rights
, for the unremitting protection of individual
rights and liberties. Once enacted, its provisions cannot easily be repealed or
amended. It must, therefore, be capable of growth and development over time to
meet new social, political and historical realities often unimagined by its
framers. The judiciary is the guardian of the constitution and must, in
interpreting its provisions, bear these considerations in mind. Professor Paul
Freund expressed this idea aptly when he admonished the American courts
"not to read the provisions of the Constitution like a last will and
testament lest it become one". [See Note 74 below]

(My emphasis)

[118] Indeed, our courts have consistently interpreted the language of our
Constitution in a dynamic fashion, in order to include legislative or
parliamentary activity that was not specifically addressed by the original
document. Our courts have done so in order to include concepts that existed or
could have existed at the time of Confederation but were not specifically
enumerated, and concepts that arose later that clearly could not have been
within the contemplation of the framers.

[119] It is to be recalled that it is trite law that the words of the B.N.A.
Act are not frozen by the framers' understandings, but rather, they must be
given a modern and flexible interpretation. As Dickson J. wrote, "there is
nothing static or frozen, narrow or technical, about the Constitution of
Canada." [See Note 75 below]

[120] If the federal power over "Marriage and Divorce" were somehow
limited by an internal definition reflecting the understandings of 1867, I
would venture to say that there would exist a significant number of unlawful
marriages in Canada today. By way of example -- as illustrated in the evidence
and materials filed -- in 1867 a husband could only petition for divorce if his
wife committed adultery. That may have been the understood definition of
divorce in 1867, but it has since clearly undergone many and repeated
legislative changes.

[121] Furthermore, if it indeed were the case that the essential nature of
marriage was that as frozen in 1867, it must now be accepted as having been
overtaken by the passage of time. By way of one example, the subordination of
the wife in the identity [page411] of the husband was absolutely central to the
legal conception of marriage in 19th-century Canada. That is obviously no
longer a view that is held by any right- thinking person in Canada.

[122] As was pointed out in the submissions, if that were still the case, it
would now be definitionally impossible for a husband to rape his wife.
Moreover, under this antiquated definition, husbands would automatically have
care and control over the children of the marriage on separation, and a wife
could not own property in her own name or sue her husband in tort. Clearly, if
one were to accept the argument advanced by the Association, there would be no
end to the mischief that reliance upon this argument could give rise to.

[123] In the end -- and as a necessary preliminary matter -- I find that the
word "Marriage" used in the
Constitution Act, 1867
does not of itself
limit the ability of Parliament to legislate same-sex marriages under head
s.
91(26)
. That is, it does not contain within it a definition that has the force
of constitutional entrenchment, and thereby requires constitutional amendment
to vary. In that regard, I find that the constitutional issue in this case is
not one that requires this court to deny jurisdiction, and that requires
amendment to the Constitution. This court has the necessary authority to
entertain the applicants' challenge and to apply the
Charter
.

[124] Finally, in answer to question one: I find that there is no statutory
impediment to the issuance of a marriage licence to same-sex couples.

(ii) Is There a Common Law Rule Preventing the Issuance of a Marriage
Licence to Same-Sex Couples?

[125] The applicant Couples and the MCCT [See Note 76 below] argument on
this issue is a relatively straightforward and simple one -- in principle. They
submit that the Canadian authorities relied upon by the respondents, such as
Matheson, [See Note 77 below] the majority decision in Layland [See Note 78
below] and EGALE [See Note 79 below] are grounded in flawed and outdated legal
principles. As a result, it is argued, there is no common law rule that
prohibits same-sex couples from marrying. The respondents and supporting
intervenors submit the contrary. [See Note 80 below] [page412]

[126] I acknowledge that the Canadian authorities just referred to are not
in and of themselves binding on this court, but they do articulate a persuasive
expression of Canadian judicial opinion. That opinion is: certain English cases
such as Hyde [See Note 81 below] and Corbett v. Corbett (orse Ashley), [See
Note 82 below] relied upon by the Canadian authorities, actually reflects the
prevailing judicial view of the common law in Canada. And, so as to be clear,
the common law rule that is expressed clearly in those Canadian authorities is
the capacity to marry is limited to "one man and one woman to the
exclusion of all others".

[127] However, while there does exist a prevalent Canadian judicial opinion
as to a common law rule, it is not a unanimous one. Greer J., in a very
thoughtful and considered dissent in Layland, departed exclusively from that
prevailing opinion. Indeed, she found that there was "no common law
prohibition against same-sex marriages in Canada". In effect, Greer J.
agreed with the submissions of the applicants in that case -- which appear to
be virtually identical to those in the within case -- and held that:

. . . the common law must grow to meet society's
expanding needs. It is clear from the supporting materials submitted by the
applicants and the intervenor Church, that gays and lesbians have been, for
many decades, entering into permanent relationships which are sanctified by
their Church. Other jurisdictions have recognized these partnerships through
legislation. [See Note 83 below]

[128] Greer J. went on to conclude that the judicial authorities relied upon
by the AGC "never really analyzes what the common law position is
regarding marriage". She goes on to resolve that the Canadian courts in
all other respects were currently and consistently expanding rights and
equalities to include gays and lesbians in the benefits that would be granted
to them through marriage. [See Note 84 below] It was generally based upon that
reasoning that Greer J. reached her conclusion.

[129] It is apparent to me that Greer J. also grounded her decision of this
issue on her considered view that a common law rule ought to reflect principles
that flow from the
Charter
. Although she emphatically states that there is no
common law rule that prohibits same-sex marriages, she goes on to buttress her
conclusion by noting that if the law is that as articulated in Hyde, it would
not [page413] withstand Charter scrutiny. [See Note 85 below] I will have more
to say on what I accept as the correctness of this process of analysis later
on.

[130] However, on the issue of an existing Canadian common law, it is with
the utmost respect that I must disagree with Greer J.'s finding in this regard.
Contrary to her conclusion, I am satisfied that there is a common law rule that
defines marriage in Canada. Indeed, I find that it is precisely that rule which
was pronounced in Matheson, as well as the majority in Layland, and most
recently in EGALE, namely, "one man and one woman to the exclusion of all
others".

[131] Merely as a point of reference, it is my observation that my finding
as to the common law definition of marriage was alluded to by the Supreme Court
in Egan v. Canada where the court was considering an issue that involved old
age security legislation and its definition of "spouse". Cory J. in
his reasons made a preliminary pronouncement about the limited scope of his
decision, and made it clear that it was not about "the societal concept of
marriage". However, he also noted that the "societal concept" or
the "traditional common law concepts of marriage" that he was
referring to was in fact the Hyde declaration as to the common law rule of
marriage. [See Note 86 below]

[132] While Egan may not be a specific pronouncement of the common law of
marriage, it is, I find, a fairly declarative statement as to the Supreme
Court's current preliminary view of what the common law likely is in Canada.
Although that is not per se a judicial pronouncement by the Supreme Court, that
suggestion taken together with the findings of the other referenced Canadian
authorities satisfy me that the Canadian common law is that derived essentially
from Hyde and Corbett.

[133] I find that there exists a Canadian common law rule that defines
marriage in Canada and it is -- "one man and one woman to the exclusion of
all others". Furthermore, the logically extrapolated result of that common
law rule is:

because it is specific to "one man and one woman", it must therefore
exclude same-sex couples.

[134] In answer to question two: I find there is a Canadian common law rule
that prevents the issuance of marriage licences to same-sex couples. Whether or
not that rule of the common law ought to be reformulated or amended is quite
another question. I turn then to question number three. [page414]

(iii) Does the Common Law Rule of Marriage Offend Certain Guarantees and
Protections to Gays and Lesbians Afforded by the
Charter
?

[135] It has been said repeatedly that courts have an obligation to ensure
that the common law evolves and develops in a manner that reflects contemporary
social reality and the values underlying the
Charter
. Greer J. in Layland
observed that the common law "does not remain static. Its very essence is
that it is able to grow to meet the expanding needs of society." She went
on to support her view with the following judicial quotation:

The object of the common law is to solve
difficulties and adjust relations in social and commercial life. It must meet,
so far as it can, sets of fact abnormal as well as usual. It must grow with the
development of the nation. It must face and deal with changing or novel
circumstances. Unless it can do that it fails in its function and declines in
its dignity and value. An expanding society demands an expanding common law.
[See Note 87 below]

[136] The applicant Couples argue that, regardless of any decision by this
court as to any remedy, it should first decide whether or not the common law
rule reflects contemporary reality. In doing so, the court should look to the
existing law's compatibility with
Charter
values. I agree.

[137] In my opinion -- regardless of the ultimate decision of this court --
any analysis of this question must include an examination of the common law
rule of marriage and its conformity with the
Charter
. The reason for this is
due to the fact that such a process is necessary to first deciding whether the
common law rule reflects contemporary social reality.

[138] A second reason for this is that, if the rule is found to be at odds
with contemporary society, the analysis is essential to the issue of remedy.
This court will then need to decide whether or not the common law rule of
marriage that is inconsistent with
Charter
protections requires reformulation
of the rule so as to comply. Or, to decide if a remedy prescribed by the
Constitution Act, 1982 is necessary because the law in its current state
actually violates the Charter. This analysis and the requirement to undertake
it are more fully explained in the examination that follows.

[139] As a point of commencement, when dealing with a common law rule, the
language of
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
will not always have any
application. That is, a court may [page415] not necessarily be required to
declare a common law rule to be "of no force and effect" merely
because it is inconsistent with the Constitution. However, the principle will
nonetheless be a significant guiding principle. For reference, that section
provides that:

The Constitution of Canada is the supreme law of
Canada, and any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the
Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency, of no force or effect.
[See Note 88 below]

[140] The authority for this just stated principle, that it may not always
be necessary to apply s. 52(1) of the Constitution Act when considering a
common law rule, is found in the Supreme Court's ruling in R. v. Swain where
Lamer C.J. observed:

. . . it is not strictly necessary to invoke
s.
52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
in order to challenge a common law,
judge-made rule on the basis of the rights and values guaranteed by the Charter
-- if a common law rule can be reformulated so as to attain its objectives
while removing any inconsistency with basic principles, a judge is entitled to
undertake such a reformulation and is not obliged to seek jurisdiction for this
action under
s. 52(1)
. [See Note 89 below]

(My emphasis)

[141] When considering a common law rule -- and relative to both the
application of
s. 52(1)
and the obligation to ensure proper growth and change
of the common law -- the Supreme Court has pronounced certain legal standards
that operate as a guide to the courts. They include:

1.
Section 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982

makes it clear that the Charter applies to the common law.

2. While the
Charter
will not apply to actions
between private litigants relying on the common law, it will apply where the
courts are developing the common law. When courts are undertaking their
inherent jurisdiction to develop the common law, the principles formulated must
be consistent with the fundamental values enshrined in the Constitution.

3. The constitutionality of a common law rule can
be scrutinized in situations where government action (or inaction) is
authorized or justified on the basis of the common law rule allegedly
infringing a
Charter
right. [page416]

4. The courts should only make those incremental
changes that are necessary to keep the common law in step with the dynamic and
evolving fabric of our society. [See Note 90 below]

[142] Given the nature of the relief sought in the case at bar -- and being
guided by the just-noted principles of law and interpretation -- my task at
this stage will be to balance two competing interests. They are, (i) the source
and purpose of the impugned common law rule that marriage is exclusive to one
man and one woman, against (ii) the rights and protections that are recognized
in the
Charter
.

[143] However, before continuing, I wish to comment on the evidence that was
placed before this court in support of the various positions that were advanced
by the parties and intervenors. The evidence generally consists of the opinions
of professed experts offering findings and conclusions drawn from their field
of expertise. This "evidence" -- perhaps not surprisingly -- is at
considerable odds with each other's interests and it covers a variety of fields
and topics. In reality, much of it -- from all the parties -- amounts to
advocacy tendered in the guise of expert testimony. I am of the opinion, and
wish to place on record that such an approach is totally unhelpful to the court
and much of the evidence is neither entitled to, nor can it be ascribed very
much weight.

[144] In addition -- and as I understand it by agreement of counsel -- and
given the nature of the process, there were no cross-examinations conducted on
most of the experts. Again, such an approach is of little assistance to the
court and is in fact problematic. Indeed, some of appearing counsel questioned
the utility of much of the material but felt they were required to present it
to the court. I would agree with the reasons for counsel's queries and had in
my mind the very same question. Nonetheless, it was generally felt that
prudence dictated that this process was necessary given the direction provided
by the Supreme Court in Miron v. Trudel,
1995 CanLII 97 (SCC)
, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 418, 124 D.L.R. (4th) 693.
[See Note 91 below]

[145] The net result is that it is not possible to properly ascribe weight
or to offer deductive reasons for questioning the credibility or reliability of
most of the experts' opinions. Nonetheless, the nature of the proceedings virtually
compels this court to consider the evidence to the best of its abilities in the
circumstances. [page417] Therefore, in addition to the evidence that I believe
I can accept, I propose that where it is appropriate to do so, I will rely upon
"judicial notice and logical reasoning" to support my conclusions and
findings. [See Note 92 below]

The source and purpose

[146] While the source of the common law rule of marriage was briefly
touched upon above -- at least to the extent of when the existing rule was
first pronounced -- the source and purpose of marriage are long and somewhat
varied. The parties in the within applications provided this court with an
abundance of opinion evidence that included historical accounts of the origins,
source and purpose of marriage. The observations and conclusions that I offer
below are derived from the evidence of each of the parties and I will generally
only touch upon and summarize the conclusions offered in that evidence.

[147] The AGC submits that the institution of marriage is an historical and
universal pre-legal concept of an opposite-sex union that was ultimately
adopted by law. It contends that there is -- and always has been -- three basic
universal norms, or "Goods and Goals" that constitutes marriage. They
are (i) procreation, (ii) fidelity, and (iii) sacrament. It argues that --
while variables may exist within marriage -- the universal norms, namely, the
Goods and Goals, always remain. Any relationship, it says, that is outside the
universal Goods and Goals does not constitute a marriage but rather an
alternative to marriage:

. . . same-sex marriage is an oxymoron, because
it lacks the universal, or defining feature of marriage according to religious,
historical, and anthropological evidence. Apart from anything else, marriage
expresses one fundamental and universal need: a setting for reproduction that
recognizes the reciprocity between nature (sexual dimorphism) and cultural
(gender complementarity). [See Note 93 below]

[148] The AGC argues that the evidence shows that marriage was, and
continues to be, the most stable unit for family formation, as opposed to, for
example, common-law unions that dissolve at the rate of 50 per cent or more. By
way of demonstrating the stability of marriage, it contends that the majority
of Canada's children -- approximately 73 per cent as at 1996 -- continue to
live in families of married couples, with women who marry having twice as many
children as those in common-law relationships: [page418]

Thus the Canadian family's awareness of itself as
a basic building block of society has not been shattered in the onrush to
postmodernity, merely weakened. . . . This review of the Canadian Postmodern
Family emphasizes the extent to which our inherited beliefs about the [strong
link of marriage to family] remain central today not only in our individual
lives but in our national identity. [See Note 94 below]

[
149
] Witnesses for the AGC offered a collective opinion that any
reformulation of the historical definition of marriage that includes the union
of same-sex couples "could have the following possible effects":

-- A profound impact on each of the universal or
nearly universal features of marriage, leading to the loss of cultural norm of
opposite-sex marriage; [See Note 95 below]

-- The further de-stabilization of marriage
privately and publicly by breaking the sense of constancy in its mission

-- "the most durable union through which to bear and raise children";
[See Note 96 below] and

-- A negative impact on women where marriage
becomes treated as a relationship between two independent adults of equal power
without an inherent core recognition that it includes the cost of child bearing
and rearing. [See Note 97 below]

[
150
] On the other hand, the applicant Couples submit that the evidence
reveals that marriage is not simply an extra-legal, pre-political institution
that exists in some essential form across all times and across all cultures.
They argue that marriage -- rather than being an unchanging, monolithic entity
-- has been a dramatically changing and variable institution. [See Note 98
below] Moreover, they submit that historically not all marriages were between
members of the opposite sexes.

[
151
] Further, the applicant Couples contend that the evidence shows that
throughout history "dozens, and probably hundreds" of societies have
recognized same-sex unions [page419] as marriages. Furthermore, same-sex
couples now have the freedom to marry in the Netherlands with Belgium to soon
follow. They point out that many other jurisdictions, including Canada,
currently provide same-sex couples with many of the same rights and obligations
as marriage, either through ascribed status or registered domestic partnership
schemes. [See Note 99 below]

[
152
] It is argued that the evidence shows that litigation seeking the
recognition of marriages of same-sex couples is part of the contemporary
history of marriage itself. They say that since the 18th century, marriage has
evolved from an arranged institution rooted in obligation, property exchange
and male control:

At the broadest of levels, marriage has evolved
from a social and economic arrangement based on a sexual division of labour in
which women were subordinate to their husbands, to a more equal union of two
people united by love and sexual intimacy, in which both partners are
frequently responsible for wage earning as well as domestic labour.
Furthermore, while in earlier times, parents had significant control over their
offspring's choice of whom to marry, given the important economic and social
consequences that flowed from the marriage arrangement, the long term movement
in Canada, as in most western countries, has been to recognize that individual
choice is the major basis for marriage. [See Note 100 below]

[
153
] In sum, the applicant Couples contend that the evidence is that
marriage is now a chosen institution that is based on companionship, love and
equal partnership. The evidence further shows that as Canadian society has
shifted from rural to urban, and from patriarchal to egalitarian -- the
institution of marriage has changed. The historical record, they say, now
demonstrates that equal access to marriage for same-sex couples is part of the
evolution of marriage in contemporary Canada.

[
154
] As I noted at the outset of this particular issue, there is much more
evidence that was tendered in support of the just stated submissions. However,
I am satisfied that what I have just set out adequately defines the parameters
or essential nature of the views of the respective parties as they relate to
the source and purpose of marriage.

[
155
] Including the above -- and after due consideration of all the
evidence, and after assessing its admissibility and weight -- there are certain
conclusions that I draw from it.

[
156
] I take no real issue with the substance and various conclusions of the
testimony and opinions offered by the parties. Indeed, I would expect that they
are all generally correct to some [page420] degree, and probably more so at
different times and to differing degrees throughout history. No doubt the
prevailing views of society at these various times are reflected in their
evidence. But it also demonstrates that both the opinions of society and
society's moral, cultural, political, and legal sense are rarely universal and
are constantly undergoing change -- even if slowly.

[
157
] I can say that whatever one gleans from the evidentiary conclusions
presented by whichever party -- marriage throughout history has mostly been
interpreted and applied as meaning opposite-sex couples. Moreover, it is beyond
dispute that there were also throughout history exceptions to this fact, and
that those exceptions included unions between members of the same sex. That, in
point of fact, is what I find to be the sum total of the source and purpose, or
the origins of marriage, that can be said to be a constant. The question for me
is, how does that square with the fundamental values of today that are
enshrined in the
Constitution Act, 1982
?

Constitutional Values

[
158
] Any analysis of constitutional values, I believe, is aided by first
re-stating some specific provisions of the
Constitution Act, 1982
. Perhaps the
most significant of these provisions is the Charter of Rights and Freedoms that
forms Part I of the Act. The Charter begins with its s. 1, which provides:

1. The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such
reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free
and democratic society. [See Note 101 below]

[
159
] It is the guarantees and protections provided by the Constitution's

Charter
, that the applicants submit are applicable, and which they claim are
infringed through the exclusion of same-sex couples from marriage. And while
there are several sections of the Charter that are said to be violated, the
right that I find to be most directly engaged by this application is the
"Equality Rights" guaranteed under
s. 15(1)
. That section reads:

15(1) Every individual is equal before and under
the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law
without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on
race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical
disability. [See Note 102 below] [page421]

[
160
] The core argument of the applicants is that lesbians, gays and
bisexuals are subjected to different treatment within the meaning of s. 15
because they do not have access to the same range of relationship options
available to heterosexuals. Specifically and simply, they argue that unlike
heterosexual couples, they are denied the freedom to marry their conjugal
partner. It is argued that this result is because the common law rule that
defines marriage distinguishes between the applicants on the basis of a
personal characteristic, namely, sexual orientation.

[
161
] The essence of the AGC submissions is that the definitional boundaries
of marriage do not engage or violate the constitutional rights of equality of
those whose unions have an essential difference. Those historical boundaries
have always been delineated as the lawful union between "one man and one
woman to the exclusion of any other person". It contends that preserving
the definition of marriage, as the descriptor of this opposite-sex institution
does not amount to discrimination. The AGC argues that the unique opposite-sex
nature of marriage does not imply that the human dignity of those in other like
relationships is diminished.

[
162
] Although the point is yet to be decided, my preliminary and cursory
view is that the very language of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
appears on its face
to make the current common law rule of marriage incompatible with it. By that I
mean -- based strictly upon sex or gender -- if marriage only includes
opposite-sex couples, it therefore excludes same-sex couples. That alone would
appear to be prima facie incompatible with Charter values and amount to a
denial of "equal benefit of the law". However, s. 15(1) has had
considerable judicial scrutiny, and the answer to the issue of equality in this
case may or may not be that simple.

The proper approach

[
163
] In order to decide whether or not the common law rule of marriage is
compatible, or in harmony, with the
Charter
, it will be necessary to measure
the two together. Since the requirement is to ascertain whether or not the law
of marriage is consistent with Charter values, the first step will be to assume
an approach that will (i) define the values that the law is alleged to offend,
and (ii) measure them against the impugned law so as to decide their
conformity.

[
164
] As I suggested above, the AGC submits that the proper approach to this
analysis is contextual. That is, it argues that marriage exists and is
universally understood to be in relation to only heterosexual unions. The core
of the purpose of the law in relation to marriage, it says, is to give legal
recognition to that [page422] primordial, socially defined, unique
relationship, in order to give collateral effect to it through the distribution
of benefits and obligations flowing from the relationship. The AGC submits that
the purpose of marriage is not to simply recognize any consenting, committed
relationship between adults -- in spite of the fact that it may have that
corresponding effect for relationships within its meaning.

[
165
] The AGC accepts that the jurisprudence makes it clear that
differential treatment that discriminates in the distribution of benefits or
obligations to couples, based upon sexual orientation is contrary to
s. 15(1)

of the
Charter
. It accepts further that this includes whether or not they are
married, and that such discrimination is based upon personal characteristics.
However, it submits that the definition of marriage does not draw a distinction
between the applicants and others in society based upon a personal
characteristic. Further, marriage does not fail to take into account any
disadvantaged position of the applicants within Canadian society that results
in substantively differential treatment between them and others on the basis of
personal characteristics.

[
166
] Moreover, the AGC contends that equality does not necessarily require
identical treatment -- rather it argues that equality is to be found in the
accommodation of differences. This principle, it is said, can be clearly found
in the comments of Iacobucci J. in Law v. Canada (Minister of Employment and
Immigration) where he writes:

. . . there may be cases where a law which
applies identically to all fails to take into account the claimant's different
traits or circumstances, yet does not infringe the claimant's human dignity in
so doing. In such cases, there could be said to be substantively differential
treatment between the claimant and others, because the law has a meaningfully
different effect upon the claimant, without there being discrimination for the
purpose of s. 15(1). [See Note 103 below]

[
167
] In response, the applicant Couples submit that the position of the AGC
amounts to an analysis based upon "definitional exclusion", which
they say is a means of analysis that has been rejected by the Supreme Court.
That is, the applicants argue that this court should not solely analyze the law
by deciding that contextually the definition of marriage means "one man and
one woman" and does not rely upon personal characteristic[s]. They say
that the underlying premise of the submission of the AGC is [page423] that
marriage is based on the ability to procreate. This, they say, is a personal
characteristic and the cause of which they are said to be excluded from
marriage, by definition.

[
168
] Unlike the AGC, the applicant Couples and the supporting intervenors
submit that the proper approach to a s. 15(1) analysis is the "purposive
approach". That is to say -- and in an effort to state the approach of
analysis in simple terms -- to answer the question: does the law offend the
purpose of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
? I agree. The purposive approach is the most
appropriate method of analysis for this most difficult issue and it is the one that
I believe allows me to arrive at the correct answer.

[
169
] Before proceeding further, I believe it will be helpful to set out
some of the basic principles and factors that I intend to be guided by.

[
170
] First, while the long history of marriage may well be that it was
almost exclusively -- although not completely -- limited to opposite-sex
couples, that by itself will not be grounds to support a
Charter
violation --
if one indeed exists. As well, a Charter violation will not be allowed to
continue simply because the consequences of overruling a discriminatory law
might be viewed by others as being novel or disturbing.

[
171
] Regarding any evidentiary standard that will apply, the law does not
require the claimants under this
s. 15(1)

Charter
challenge to demonstrate that
the impugned distinction amounts to unreasonableness, or that it is
"invidious, unfair or irrational". [See Note 104 below] All that is
required is for the applicants to show that the impugned law treats them more
harshly than others. It is not a question of degree.

[
172
] And finally, it does not matter whether it was the law's intention to
discriminate specifically against gays and lesbians. It may well be a debatable
point, but I suspect that historically, and especially at various times, the
law was intended to do just that. In my opinion -- and leaving aside whether or
not it discriminates -- it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the
common law of marriage does what it has generally always intended, namely, to
allow "one man and one woman" to marry and "to exclude all
others".

[
173
] It is not my intention to review the entire history of judicial
examination of the guaranteed right under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
. Rather, in setting
out my analysis I will simply rely on the most recent principles that are set
out by Iacobucci J. in Law. I feel comfortable in doing so because much of the
history of the [page424] relevant judicial consideration was reviewed by him in
that case and I believe the most reliable considerations to be applied to the
purposive approach are to be found in his reasons.

[
174
] At the outset, I believe the purpose of the s. 15(1) equality
guarantee is worth repeating. While it has been described in somewhat different
language by different justices of the Supreme Court it has always been
described by reference to the very lofty values it is intended to reflect in
Canada. For my purposes, I prefer the language of McIntyre J. that was
referenced by Iacobucci J. in Law:

. . . the purpose of s. 15(1) is to promote a
society in which all are secure in the knowledge that they are recognized at
law as human beings equally deserving of concern, respect and consideration.
The provision is a guarantee against evil oppression . . . designed to remedy
the imposition of unfair limitations upon opportunities, particularly for those
persons or groups who have been subject to historical disadvantage, prejudice,
and stereotyping.

[
175
] An analysis undertaken by the court in accordance with the purposive
approach involves a three-step process. Specifically, a claimant must
demonstrate that:

1. The impugned law subjects the applicants to
differential treatment. That is, the law denies them equal benefit or equal
protection: that it treats them differently as compared to other persons or
groups.

2. The differential treatment is based on one or
more of the enumerated or analogous grounds set out in s. 15(1).

3. The differential treatment operates in a
substantive sense. That is, it imposes a burden upon, or withholds a benefit
from, the applicants. And that it does so in an unacceptable manner in that it
perpetuates or promotes the view that the applicants are less worthy as a
member of Canadian society, not equally deserving of concern, respect and
consideration. [See Note 105 below]

[
176
] I wish to note at this time that if this court finds that the meaning
of marriage subjects the applicants to differential treatment -- the AGC
concedes that the sexual orientation of the applicants is the basis for such
different treatment. Additionally, the AGC agrees that this is an analogous
ground under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
. [page425]

[
177
] Finally, to determine whether the law has the effect of demeaning the
dignity of the applicant Couples, I am required to look at "contextual
factors" and examine them from the perspective of the applicant Couples.
My focus will be both subjective and objective with the relevant point being
the view of the reasonable person in circumstances the same as the applicant
Couples.

[
178
] Contextual factors that are to be considered by a court are not
exhaustive and some of them include:

-- Pre-existing disadvantage, stereotyping,
prejudice, or vulnerability experienced by the individual or group at issue.
Although this factor is not per se an infringement, its existence will favour a
finding of a s. 15(1) breach.

-- Does the impugned law take into account the
claimant's actual situation? That is, does it harmonize with or speak to the
issues of the complaint?

-- The ameliorative purpose or effects of the
impugned law upon a more disadvantaged person or group in society. In other
words, on balance, do the law's benefits to the group it applies, exceed the
needs of the group excluded from it?

-- The nature and scope of the interest affected by
the impugned law. The harsher the law is on the affected group the more likely
that the differential treatment responsible for these consequences is
discriminatory. [See Note 106 below]

[
179
] With that as a background, I will now proceed to set out my analysis.

The perspective of the applicants

[
180
] The proper perspective that is advanced by the applicants as being the
correct one from which this court should examine this issue includes certain
undeniable truths. They submit it begins with the fact that lesbians, gays and
bisexuals are subjected to differential treatment within the meaning of
s. 15

of the
Charter
because they do not have access to the same range of
relationship options available to heterosexuals. Specifically, they say they
are denied the right and freedom to marry their conjugal partner.

[
181
] Once again, the contention of the applicants is that the common law
distinguishes between the applicants and others on the basis of a personal
characteristic, namely, sexual orientation. [page426] They submit that some of
the effects of the denial of equal marriage include:

-- Just as participation in civil marriage would
communicate a powerful message of inclusion in civil society, the denial of the
freedom to marry causes numerous, egregious harms. It threatens the well being
and psychological integrity of all gays and lesbians, their children and
society at large.

-- Exclusion from civil marriage threatens the
psychological integrity and sense of self-worth of lesbians and gays. Denial of
equal marriage also serves to justify the legitimacy of cultural heterosexism,
thus perpetuating prejudice and violence against lesbians, gays, and bisexuals.

-- Civil marriage is required to respect and
promote the equality of lesbians and gays. If the applicant Couples succeed
only in securing equivalent rights and obligations that pertain to marriage,
but are denied the status of civil marriage itself, discrimination will be
permitted. Given the social, political and historical context of lesbians and
gays, only equal access to civil marriage will meet the requirements of the

Charter
.

-- The social context includes the increasing
tolerance and even acceptance of gays and lesbians in society, here and in
other democracies.

-- For Christians, marriage is founded on love, and
on freedom of choice. As with many other Canadians, for members of the MCCT the
capacity to marry and the right to marry the person of one's choice is an
incident of full membership in society, of "full personhood".

-- Marriage for Christians is a manifestation of
religious belief, a commitment before and to God. It is a spiritual
celebration. Gays and lesbians have been marginalized in our society, including
by religious bodies. It is important to note the key role of the MCCT in the
lesbian and gay community as a spiritual haven, a refuge for those who have
been made to feel unwelcome in other faiths because of their sexual
orientation. Marriage is a public affirmation of love before friends and family,
and often, within a religious congregation. It is a status with well recognized
social significance that, rightly or wrongly, is perceived by many to be the
commitment of the highest order of one person to another. [page427]

[
182
] It is from this context as viewed by the applicants that I will now go
on to examine whether or not the common law rule of marriage is compatible with

s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
. And to repeat -- as I noted at the outset of this
question -- the following examination is necessary for me to decide whether,
(i) the reformulation of the common law of marriage is required, or (ii) a
constitutional remedy is necessary.

Differential treatment

[
183
] As noted earlier, the AGC takes the position that the common law rule
of marriage does not differentiate. It argues that any distinction in this case
is one that is inherently tied to the concept of the institution, or
definition, per se, and is not a distinction envisaged by the meaning of
s. 15

of the
Charter
.

[
184
] Additionally the AGC submits that the
Charter
guarantees the equal
protection and benefit of the law, not the right to nomenclature. It argues
that not being able to obtain the label of "married" does not
constitute a distinction based on a personal characteristic. Rather, it says it
relates to the incapacity of their unique relationship to meet the core,
opposite-sex, definitional requirements of marriage. In this sense, it says
that by capturing the essence of marriage, the common law recognizes the
inherent differences between opposite-sex and same-sex relationships. [See Note
107 below]

[
185
] The AGC goes on to submit that, since the recent enactment of the

Modernization of Benefits and Obligations Act
, same-sex couples receive
substantive equal benefit and protection of the federal law. It says that
same-sex couples are -- insofar as benefits are concerned -- no longer in a
disadvantaged position within Canadian society as compared to opposite-sex
couples. [See Note 108 below] In this regard, it is said that, to the extent
that distinctions in treatment between married couples and non-married
common-law couples remain, they are insignificant. In any case, the argument
goes, any distinctions in treatment, when properly considered, can either be
justified or remedied by individual amendment so as to provide immediate access
to any residual benefits and protections engaged by marriage.

[
186
] Respectfully, I find that I must disagree with the submissions and
conclusions of the AGC. I do so for a variety of reasons. [page428]

[
187
] The gist of the first part of AGC's submissions requires this court to
accept that "marriage" is a word that merely identifies a unique
institution. That argument implies that, if the applicants are granted all the
rights, privileges and benefits of the institution of marriage -- but under
some other nomenclature -- then there can be no discrimination because there
would be no differential treatment. That, in my opinion, is wrong.

[
188
] Marriage is more than nomenclature -- more than just a word. One could
say that the first indicator of its importance is the fact that this lengthy
and complex court hearing apparently had to occur. In my opinion, the passion
and sincerity of all those who argued before this court is testament to the
deeply held views of marriage. The applicants fervently plead to be included in
that institution: the respondents intensely plead to protect its exclusivity. I
am entirely convinced that marriage is much more than a word and I would agree
with the observation that marriage -- to most of Canadian society is:

. . . the institution that accords to a union the
profound social stamp of approval and acceptance of the relationship as being
of the highest value. [See Note 109 below]

[
189
] I also agree with those others who describe it as being:

. . . legal, religious, social, vocational, and
personal . . . The power of marriage comes not from what it is in the abstract,
or how it is defined, or even what it symbolizes, but from how it is
transubstantiated by society's focus on marital status as key element in
defining every person. [See Note 110 below]

[
190
] In Egan, Cory J. and Iacobucci J. were of the opinion that a law that
offers a "significant choice" may also offer a "valuable
benefit". And where the definition of that law confers state recognition
of the legitimacy of a particular status, denial of the ability to choose that
status to lesbians and gays amounts to a violation of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.
[See Note 111 below] That, I find, is what has occurred in the case at bar.

[
191
] In support of my conclusion, I return once again to Greer J.'s.
decision in Layland for assistance and in particular where she examined some of
the judicial pronouncements on s. 15(1) as they [page429] existed in 1993.
Relying on the language of Wilson J. in R. v. Turpin, [See Note 112 below]
Greer J. expressed a conclusion that I agree with, namely:

One cannot look simply within the four corners of
what pre-
Charter
cases held was a marriage. It is important that the issue be
properly placed in the larger social context of our modern-day society and its
mores and expectations.

The
Charter
cases show that our courts have found
that "choice" is a benefit of the law. In the case at bar, the
applicants have been denied their right to choose whom they wish to marry. In
my view, the right to choose is a fundamental right and applies to the context
of marriage in our society.

It is a basic theory in our society that the
state will respect choices made by individuals and the state will avoid
subordinating these choices to any one conception. [See Note 113 below] An
individual's s. 15 guarantees are designed to protect the individual's right to
choose. Our courts and the state have always attempted to redress historic
prejudice and bigotry through the application of the law. In my view, this is
what the
Charter
was intended to do. [See Note 114 below]

[
192
] I also reject the argument of the AGC that the benefits afforded
through the institution of marriage can be remedied by amendment to legislation
that otherwise grants benefits to co- habiting couples. In my opinion, that
submission amounts to the "separate but equal" argument that has long
since been rejected in Canada as a justification for an otherwise discriminatory
law. [See Note 115 below]

[
193
] I find that it is [a] non-answer to the concerns of the applicants to
simply say to them that same-sex couples have -- or will have -- all the
benefits that married couples have through other legislative measures such as
"domestic partners". [See Note 116 below]

[
194
] To accept that argument would mean that I agree that same-sex couples
are entitled to all the benefits and privileges that opposite-sex couples are
granted through marriage, but not the right to be recognized as married. In
other words, I would have to embrace the concept that same-sex couples are
entitled to be married; they just cannot appropriate the word marriage because
that belongs exclusively to heterosexual couples. That would be a wrong concept
for this court to embrace.

[
195
] It should be recalled that at one time African- Americans were
entitled to sit on the same bus as "whites" and in seats that were
equally comfortable to other seats. They just could not sit at [page430] the
front of the bus because those equal seats were reserved for "white
people". As well, African-Americans were entitled to drink water and to
use toilet facilities that were in all other respects equal to those used by
white people. Once again, they could not do so from the same fountain or use
the same toilet as whites. Each of those were -- although once seemingly
credible concepts -- discredited and rejected by courts in the United States.

[
196
] In Andrews, our Supreme Court -- with equal judicial emphasis --
rejected such a doctrine in Canada. [See Note 117 below] On that issue, I agree
with and adopt the language of Linden J.A. in his dissent in Egan v. Canada who
found that:

One cannot avoid the conclusion that offering
benefits to gay and lesbian partners under a different scheme from heterosexual
partners is a version of the separate but equal doctrine. That appalling
doctrine must not be resuscitated in Canada [four] decades after its
much-heralded death in the United States. [See Note 118 below]

[
197
] In conclusion, I find that the answer to this first aspect of the
s.
15(1)

Charter
analysis is -- the common law rule of marriage subjects the
applicants to different treatment than others. That is to say, I find that
lesbians and gays are treated differently than heterosexuals when they are
denied the right to enter into the societal institution of marriage.

Analogous ground

[
198
] As noted above in para. 176, the AGC agrees that if there is a finding
of different treatment, it is grounded in sexual orientation, which is an analogous
ground under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
. As I find that to be indeed the case, I
correspondingly answer this part of the analysis in the affirmative.

Is it substantive differential treatment?

[
199
] It is argued that by deeming gay and lesbian people to be excluded
from marriage, there is a denial of their equal opportunity to fully
participate in our society. There is, it is contended, a fundamental right to
marry recognized in Canadian, United States and international jurisprudence. I
fully accept this argument and agree that:

. . . the decision of whether or not to marry
can, indeed, be one of the most personal decisions an individual will ever make
over the course of his or her [page431] lifetime. It can be as fundamental, as
momentous, and as personal as a choice regarding, for instance, one's
citizenship or even one's religion. [See Note 119 below]

[
200
] The first contextual factor I need to consider under this analysis is
to decide whether there subsists within Canadian society a "pre-existing disadvantage,
vulnerability, stereotyping, or prejudice" experienced by gay and lesbian
people. In my opinion, this issue has little to no contrary argument -- it most
assuredly does exist.

[
201
] Our courts have often recognized that same-sex relationships have not
been given equal concern, respect, and consideration. I agree with the view
that the denial of equal marriage can -- and no doubt does -- reflect and
reinforce existing, inaccurate understandings of the merits, capabilities and
worth of lesbian and gay relationships within Canadian society. Further, I
agree that, given that this occurs, it must have the effect of resulting in
further stigmatization.

[
202
] Excluding gays and lesbians from marriage disregards the needs,
capacities and circumstances of same-sex spouses and their children. It
declares an entire class of persons unworthy of the recognition and support of
state sanction for their marriages. In sum, marriage -- as it is currently
defined -- fails to harmonize with or take into account the issues of gays and
lesbians.

[
203
] The next contextual factor that must be addressed is whether the
denial has an "ameliorative purpose" or effect. Once again, the AGC
argues that marriage is a deep-rooted and unique social institution that is
recognized by the Supreme Court as such. The AGC asserts that it is of
fundamental importance to all societies in that it provides a means --
admittedly not the only one -- of serving and recognizing the realities of one
of the goals of marriage, namely -- the nurturing and protection of children.
It adds that, as the vast majority of children continue to be the natural
offspring of their parents' heterosexual relationships, these relationships are
recognized as having special needs with which the legislatures and courts have
justifiably been concerned.

[
204
] In my opinion, the relationships that our Supreme Court has been
concerned with -- although no doubt mostly consisting of heterosexual couples
-- are not exclusively opposite-sex couple relationships. I believe recent
decisions of the court bear testament to that fact. To the contrary, the court
is specifically and [page432] rightly concerned with "family
relationships" that consist of parents and children. Same-sex couples who
form family units with children are no less parents and are no less entitled to
the same concerns by our courts.

[
205
] Indeed, in some of those cases -- such as Law and Vriend v. Alberta --
the Supreme Court found that an underinclusive benefit like civil marriage
recognition that "excludes from its scope the members of an historically
disadvantaged group will rarely escape the charge of discrimination". [See
Note 120 below] I find that to be precisely the case in the within
applications.

[
206
] The final contextual factor focuses on an examination of the nature
and scope of the interest affected by the impugned law. That is, how harshly
does the law of marriage affect gays and lesbians by their exclusion from it?
This analysis includes an examination of the fundamental nature and broad scope
of marriage, measured against the discriminatory impact of the denial of equal
marriage to the applicants. As was noted in Law:

[T]he discriminatory calibre of differential
treatment cannot be fully appreciated without evaluating not only the economic
but also the constitutional and societal significance attributed to the
interest or interests adversely affected by the legislation in question.
Moreover, it is relevant to consider whether the distinction restricts access
to a fundamental social institution, or affects "a basic aspect of full
membership in Canadian society", or "constitute[s] a complete
non-recognition of a particular group". [See Note 121 below]

[
207
] As previously noted, it appears to be universally accepted that the
freedom to marry the person of one's choice and the right to have that
relationship recognized by society is of fundamental importance in our society.
By way of comparison, in M. v. H., Cory J. recognized both the tangible and
symbolic impact of the denial of access to the protections of the spousal
support scheme:

The societal significance of the benefit
conferred by the statute cannot be overemphasized. The exclusion of same-sex
partners from the benefits of s. 29 of the FLA promotes the view that M., and
individuals in same-sex relationships generally, are less worthy of recognition
and protection. It implies that they are judged to be incapable of forming
intimate relationships of economic interdependence as compared to opposite-sex
couples, without regard to their actual circumstances. As the intervener EGALE
submitted, such exclusion perpetuates the disadvantages suffered by individuals
in same-sex relationships and contributes to the erasure of their existence.
[See Note 122 below] [page433]

[
208
] I expect that few could, or would, disagree with the notion that equal
access to marriage is at least commensurate with, and perhaps even more
fundamental and important than, spousal support. There are distinct and
profound benefits in marriage, which as I noted previously are not satisfied
merely by providing equivalent economic benefits, rights and obligations
through some other means. Simply put, such alternative methods do not have the
same meaning or significance as access to them by right of entry to a basic social
and cultural institution.

[
209
] By way of illustration, L'Heureux-Dubé J., in her dissenting opinion
in Egan, found that the same-sex claimants in that case did not suffer economic
prejudice from their distinction in connection with Old Age Security
legislation. However, she did find that, because the claimants were excluded
"as a couple" from those in relationships "analogous to
marriage" -- that amounted to an interest that was worthy of
Charter

protection. She expressed the interest as being:

. . . an important facet of full and equal
membership in Canadian society. Given the marginalized position of homosexuals
in society, the metamessage that flows almost inevitably from excluding
same-sex couples from such an important social institution is essentially that
society considers such relationships to be less worthy of respect, concern and
consideration than relationships involving members of the opposite sex. This
fundamental interest is therefore severely and palpably affected by the
impugned distinction. [See Note 123 below]

[
210
] If the conclusion of L'Heureux-Dubé J. in Egan is valid in the
circumstances of that case -- and I agree that it is -- then it must be more
than equally correct for the social institution of marriage. I therefore find that
the denial of equal marriage violates
s. 15
of the
Charter
. Specifically, I
find that it draws a distinction in a substantive sense on the basis of sex and
sexual orientation that withholds the equal benefit of the law in a manner that
offends the human dignity of gays, lesbians and bisexuals.

(iv) Are There Other Sections of the
Charter
, Such as Sections 2 and 7,
Which are Violated?

[
211
] Given my just-stated findings and conclusions in respect of
s. 15(1)

of the
Charter
, I do not believe it is strictly necessary for disposing of
these applications that I also consider other rights and guarantees afforded by
the Charter. However -- and [page434] although it may not be a requirement -- I
believe the overall interest in, and importance of the issues requires, that I
make some observations and comments about some of the other Charter provisions.
What follows includes those observations and comments -- but only in brief.

[
212
] It is my view that of all the submissions made in this case, any other
rights infringements that could be relied upon would occur through violations
of subsections 2(a) and (b), namely, "freedom of religion" and
"freedom of opinion and expression". I find that the arguments
directed at violations of s. 2(d), being "freedom of association",
and
s. 7
of the
Charter
are not applicable in the within applications and are
rejected.

Freedom of religion (s. 2(a))

[
213
] I find that in order for the applicants to succeed, they need to show
that the law in some way compels or constrains the applicants' right to
distinct religious beliefs and practices. The MCCT declares that the definition
of marriage in Canada offends religious freedom because the state purports to
extend the sanction of traditional churches into the MCCT's sanctuary. This, it
says, is the effect by the state's refusal to recognize marriages that conform
to MCCT's doctrine while honouring the marriage doctrine of other "more
traditional churches".

[
214
] State recognition of a church's marriage ritual, MCCT argues, provides
an "endorsement" of the legitimate status of that church, legally and
socially. Conversely, not recognizing the beliefs and practices of another
church amounts to non- sanction of those beliefs and practices by the state.
Respectfully, I disagree.

[
215
] Not all civil marriages are recognized by religious institutions, just
as not all of them can be solemnized as a civil marriage under Canadian law.
While the definition of marriage may hold religious significance for some
Canadians, it does not follow that Canada is therefore obliged to give
recognition to all religious definitions of marriage. In my view, failure to
provide state recognition through civil recognition of all forms of religious
marriage does not constitute constraint within the meaning of
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
. Indeed, there is in fact no state action that can be complained of in
the within case.

[
216
] It seems to me that the claim of the MCCT is analogous to the one made
in Adler v. Ontario where the Supreme Court considered whether Ontario was
obliged by s. 2(a) to provide public funding to foster and facilitate religious
education for all diverse religious groups in the province. The court rejected
the claim on the grounds that s. 2(a) enshrined no right to positive [page435]
state facilitation of religious practice or belief. [See Note 124 below] As I
said, that appears to me to be the same in this case. That is, the state should
not be required to advance any particular definition of marriage that must be
adhered to by any religious faith.

[
217
