] Furthermore, the definition of marriage does not protect one religion
over another. Rather, I believe that it has the same impact on individual
members of the MCCT as it does on same-sex couples belonging to other
denominations that may celebrate or formalize their relationships within their
own denominations.

Freedom of opinion and expression (s. 2(b))

[
218
] Once again, I find that this section of the
Charter
is not engaged
because, once again, there is no state action that interferes with the applicant's
freedom of expression. On this point, I agree with Pittfield J. in EGALE where
he concludes that this section guarantees everyone the freedom of thought,
belief, opinion and expression. I agree that what is guaranteed by this is the
freedom to think the thoughts and hold the opinions one wishes to think or
hold, and to express those thoughts or opinions orally or in writing. [See Note
125 below] That is not the case at bar.

[
219
] I believe that the words "freedom of expression" can be
appropriate to describe the formalization of the legal relationship that is
marriage whether same-sex or opposite-sex. However, there is nothing in the
evidence to suggest that any aspect of legal marriage affects or restricts the
freedom of gays or lesbians to specifically express their love or commitment to
a chosen partner. In my view,
s. 2(b)
of the
Charter
is also not appropriately
engaged in the circumstances of the within case.

(v) Is There a Section 1 Charter Analysis Required and, if so, Can the
Infringement be Justified?

[
220
] The applicants take the position that because the impugned law is
judge-made common law, no
s. 1

Charter
analysis is required. For ease of
reference s. 1 provides that:

1. The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such
reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free
and democratic society.

[
221
] As can be observed strictly from the language, s. 1 has two separate
and distinct functions. First, it constitutionally guarantees [page436] the
rights and freedoms set forth within the
Charter
. And second, it sets out the
criteria required to justify any limits on those rights and freedoms should any
be infringed. Thus, it is only where a claimant's Charter rights have been
infringed through limits prescribed by law that the court is required to
consider s. 1. If such a limitation is established then, it can only pass
judicial scrutiny if it can be demonstrably justified as being reasonable.

Requirement of a s. 1 analysis

[
222
] I have found that the common law rule regarding marriage infringes the
applicants' s. 15 equality rights. In such an eventuality -- and contrary to
the position taken by the applicants -- the AGC contends that I must go on and
conduct a
s. 1

Charter
analysis. Their reasons for their respective positions
follow.

[
223
] The AGC's position that a
s. 1

Charter
analysis must be undertaken, it
says, is supported by two separate propositions. The first is that the Supreme
Court states clearly that -- even though a court is considering a judge-made
rule of the common law -- it must nonetheless conduct a justification analysis
under s. 1 of the Charter. The second submission is that, in any case, because
Parliament has clearly indicated its legislative intent in the
Modernization of
Benefits and Obligations Act
, [See Note 126 below] it has therefore in effect
"prescribed by law" the common law definition of marriage. In support
for this second proposition, the AGC points to the language of Le Dain J. in R.
v. Therens where he wrote:

The requirement that the limit be prescribed by
law is chiefly concerned with the distinction between a limit imposed by law
and one that is arbitrary. The limit will be prescribed by law within the
meaning of s. 1 if it is expressly provided for by statute or regulation, or
results by necessary implication from the terms of a statute or regulation or
from its operating requirements. The limit may also result from the application
of a common law rule. [See Note 127 below]

[
224
] The applicants submit that a
s. 1

Charter
analysis is not necessary
because, they say, any law -- including a common law rule -- on which
government action is based is of no force or effect if it is inconsistent with
the Charter. Moreover, they contend that the courts must amend it given that
they were responsible for fashioning the common law rule that infringes Charter
rights. Simply put, the core of their submission on this point is simply -- there
is no impugned legislative provision for the court to strike down, read in, or
read down. They contend that a common [page437] law rule is wholly judge- made
law and, accordingly, it is not necessary to attempt to justify the rights
violation.

[
225
] A further submission of the applicants is that the proper approach is
for the court to cure the infringement by fashioning a new rule that complies
with constitutional requirements. In support of this submission, they direct
this court to certain judicial pronouncements of the Supreme Court.

[
226
] One particular pronouncement -- although in the context of examining a
common law rule that was found to violate
s. 7
of the
Charter
-- is said to be
where Lamer C.J. in Swain offered the opinion that:

. . . because this appeal involves a
Charter

challenge to a common law, judge-made rule, the Charter analysis involves
somewhat different considerations than would apply to a challenge to a
legislative provision. For example, having found that the existing common law
rule limits an accused's rights under
s. 7
of the Charter, it may not be
strictly necessary to go on to consider the application of s. 1. . . . It
could, in my view, be appropriate to consider at this stage whether an
alternative common law rule could be fashioned which would not be contrary to
the principles of fundamental justice.

. . . I can see no conceptual problem with the
court's simply enunciating such a rule to take the place of the old rule,
without considering whether the old rule could nonetheless be upheld under
s. 1

of the
Charter
. Given that the common law rule was fashioned by judges and not
by Parliament or a legislature, judicial deference to elected bodies is not an
issue. If it is possible to reformulate a common law rule so that it will not
conflict with the principles of fundamental justice, such a reformulation
should be undertaken. [See Note 128 below]

[
227
] At the outset, it is apparent to me through the language of Lamer C.J.
just referred to, that the relevant principle is not declaratory. That is, in
the context of the within case, this court is not strictly bound to -- nor is
it precluded from -- undertaking a
s. 1

Charter
analysis simply because the
impugned law is a judge-made common law rule and not legislation. As I shall demonstrate
later in these reasons, it is possible and I believe appropriate for this court
to reformulate the impugned common law rule to enable it to conform to the
principles of fundamental justice.

[
228
] And, although in my opinion I do not believe a
s. 1

Charter
analysis
is strictly necessary in this case -- however, again given the high degree of
importance of this decision, I have decided that one ought to nonetheless be
undertaken.

Section 1 analysis

[
229
] As s. 1 of the
Charter
makes clear, where a law gives rise to a
Charter breach, it must then be demonstrably justified as a [page438]
reasonable limit in a free and democratic society in order for it to pass
judicial scrutiny.

[
230
] The test for establishing that a limit prescribed by law is "reasonable"
and "demonstrably justified" in a free and democratic society is
found in the seminal case of R. v. Oakes. [See Note 129 below] The Oakes test
was recently restated by Bastarache J. in Thomson Newspapers Co. v. Canada
(Attorney General). [See Note 130 below] It is a two-pronged test that requires
(i) an initial examination of the objective or concerns of the law that is
responsible for the limits on the complainants'
Charter
rights, and then (ii)
an examination of the said objective or concerns to determine:

(i) Whether the objective or concern is
sufficiently important to warrant overriding the protected right. The objective
or concern must be pressing and substantial;

(ii) Whether it does so proportionately. Proportionality is measured through
a three-part test that requires that the measures chosen:

(a) are rationally connected to the objective;

(b) impair the right or freedom as little as
possible; and

(c) result in harmful effects, if any, that are
proportional to both the law's salutary effects and the importance of the
objective.

[
231
] The onus of justifying an infringement of a
Charter
right rests with
the party seeking to uphold the law -- in this case the AGC. In RJR-MacDonald
Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General), the Supreme Court noted the degree of the
burden on both the party seeking to justify the law and that which the court
must insist upon. In the words of McLachlin J.:

. . . the state must show that the violative law
is "demonstrably justified." The choice of the word "demonstrably"
is critical. The process is not one of mere intuition, nor is it one of
deference to Parliament's choice. It is a process of demonstration. This
reinforces the notion inherent in the word "reasonable" of rational
inference from evidence or established truths. [See Note 131 below]

(Original emphasis) [page439]

She went on to state:

[The courts must] . . . insist that before the
state can override constitutional rights, there must be a reasoned
demonstration of the good which the law may achieve in relation to the
seriousness of the infringement. It is the task of the courts to maintain this
bottom line if the rights conferred by our constitution are to have force and
meaning. The task is not easily discharged, and may require the courts to
confront the tide of popular public opinion. But that has always been the price
of maintaining constitutional rights. [See Note 132 below]

[
232
] I turn now to my consideration of the just-stated test. And -- given
my decision earlier that a
s. 1

Charter
analysis was not authoritatively
necessary given the foundation of the law in question -- my examination of the
various parts of the Oakes test will not be as extensive as might otherwise be
appropriate. Nonetheless it is my intention to conduct a review and analysis of
this test by being concise yet clear.

(i) The objective and its importance

[
233
] Once again -- and as I previously noted above -- the AGC submits that
the restriction against same-sex marriage flows from the objective, or the
"Goods and Goals", of marriage, which it contends is essentially to
further procreation and provide institutional support to families with
children. The AGC argues that same-sex partners are excluded from marriage
because they do not have the biological capacity to conceive a child together.

[
234
] The applicants and the concurring intervenors submit that the
historical record falls short of supporting the contention that procreation is
the core purpose or objective of marriage. They argue that it was only recently
that same-sex couples began to advance claims for equal recognition of their
conjugal relationships, including equal access to marriage. It is, they assert,
only then that some courts began to identify procreation as the essential
purpose of marriage. The aspect of procreation, they say, is now advanced
through convenience. Historically, it was not considered essential to the
validity of marriage and capacity to marry during the early development of the
common law rule.

[
235
] Casting aside all other arguments, the infringing objective of the
common law rule in this case -- in as condensed a fashion as I can fairly state
it when stripped of all its peripheral features -- is one that distils down to
the issue of procreation. The question for me therefore in response to the
first issue under the second branch of the test is:

whether the objective of procreation is of sufficient importance to override
the applicants'
s. 15

Charter
rights. That is, [page440] is the exclusion of
lesbians and gays from entering into the institution of marriage because of the
perceived inability of them to naturally procreate pressing and substantial?

[
236
] Once again -- since the impugned law exists at common law -- the task
of this court is to determine the reasoning of the courts that created the
rights limitation in the first place (i.e. the exclusion of same-sex couples
from marriage). I do not intend to brief the relevant judicial authorities on
this issue, although I have set out the essence of them above. [See Note 133
below] I will say by way of general comment that if the foundation of those
decisions is rooted in procreation -- it must be inferred because it is
certainly not clear from the reasons.

[
237
] As the language of
s. 1
of the
Charter
dictates, in order to be
sufficiently pressing and substantial to justify infringement or denial of a
constitutionally protected right, the objective of the limitation must be
consistent with the values of a free and democratic society. Dickson J. in
Oakes offered an impression of some of what makes up a free and democratic
society. He wrote:

The Court must be guided by the values and
principles essential to a free and democratic society which I believe embody,
to name but a few, respect for the inherent dignity of the human person,
commitment to social justice and equality, accommodation of a wide variety of
beliefs, respect for cultural and group identity, and faith in social and
political institutions which enhance the participation of individuals and
groups in society. The underlying values and principles of a free and
democratic society are the genesis of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the

Charter
and the ultimate standard against which a limit on a right or freedom
must be shown, despite its effect, to be reasonable and demonstrably justified.
[See Note 134 below]

[
238
] I do not agree that the evidence -- such as it is -- supports the
AGC's proposition that procreation is the essential objective of marriage.
Indeed, the evidence actually demonstrates that it was only recently -- when
same-sex couples began to advance claims for equal recognition of their
conjugal relationships -- that some courts began to infer that procreation was
an essential component to marriage. There is simply no evidence that convinces
me that those earlier courts, when developing the common law rules regarding
the validity of marriage and capacity, viewed procreation as the purpose of
marriage.

[
239
] By way of example, it is well-established in annulment cases that a
marriage is valid and not voidable despite the fact that one spouse refuses to
have sexual intercourse, or is infertile, or insists on using contraceptives
when having sexual intercourse. [page441] These cases demonstrate to my
satisfaction that procreation has not been considered by the courts to be a
factor at all. They especially do not provide authority for the proposition
that it was the sole or primary purpose of the matrimonial contract.

[
240
] I reach the same conclusion when I look to those cases where a husband
is unable to consummate the marriage due to impotence resulting from advanced
age. In those cases, Canadian courts have consistently ruled that the marriage
is understood to be for the purpose of "companionship" and is
therefore valid, and not voidable. This finding is made in spite of the fact of
the spouses' inability to have sexual intercourse and thus an inability to
procreate. [See Note 135 below]

[
241
] Further still, in 1948 the House of Lords in the case of Baxter v.
Baxter explicitly held that procreation is not the principal end of marriage.
In Baxter, a man sought to annul his marriage on the ground of non-consummation
because his wife refused to have sexual intercourse with him unless he used a
condom. The House of Lords denied the annulment and -- although the court
expressed the view that raising children in a family of a particular faith was
the essence of marriage -- it added:

In any view of Christian marriage the essence of
the matter, as it seems to me, is that the children, if there be any, should be
born into a family, as that word is understood in Christendom generally, and in
the case of a marriage between spouses of a particular faith that they should
be brought up and nurtured in that faith. But this is not the same thing as
saying . . . that procreation of children is the principal end of marriage.
[See Note 136 below]

(My emphasis)

[
242
] In sum, I do [not] accept that the objective of procreation is a basis
that can support the restriction against same-sex marriage. Rather, it could be
reasonably argued -- as it has been by the applicants -- that it appears to be
a mere pretext used to rationalize discrimination against lesbians and gays.

[
243
] One could reasonably reach the conclusion that the real, although
unstated, purpose of the restriction is to preserve the exclusive privileged
status of heterosexual conjugal relationships in society. If that was an
underlying purpose -- and I do not go so far as to decide that it is -- it
could not be justified in a free and democratic society. Moreover, given that
such an objective would of itself be discriminatory and contrary to
Charter

values, it could not be construed as being pressing or substantial. Any
justification based upon the belief that heterosexual relationships are
superior to same-sex relationships would be rejected as being
"fundamentally [page442] repugnant, because it would justify the law upon
the very basis upon which it is attacked for violating" the Charter right.
[See Note 137 below]

[
244
] In Vriend, the Supreme Court remarked that "the legislative omission
[of sexual orientation] is on its face the very antithesis of the principles
involved in the legislation as a whole." [See Note 138 below] In Rosenberg
v. Canada (Attorney General), the Ontario Court of Appeal held that the failure
to include same-sex cohabitants in the definition of "spouse" had the
objective of favouring heterosexual unions. The court held that such a failure
amounted to an objective that was "discriminatory and cannot be viewed as
justification for constitutional violation". [See Note 139 below]

[
245
] In the end -- and as I said earlier -- the AGC has failed to satisfy
me that procreation is the reason for the common law rule of marriage.
Therefore, and further to the analysis, it fails the evidentiary onus to show
that procreation is a pressing and substantial concern or objective of the rule
of marriage. No other objective has been established to my satisfaction that is
sufficiently important such that it warrants overriding the guaranteed rights
of gays and lesbians.

[
246
] Given the failure of the evidentiary burden, I find that the current
common law rule of marriage is one that is based upon sexual orientation and is
intended to specifically exclude marriage between same-sex couples. This, in
turn, is categorically a rights violation based upon a discriminatory
objective. Altogether, the initial step of the Oakes test has not been made
out.

(ii) Is the infringement proportional to the
objective?

[
247
] Because of my just-stated conclusion regarding the first branch of the
Oakes test, it is unnecessary for me to analyze the second branch. However, as
before, given the significance and high degree of interest in this matter and
to more fully decide it, I believe some analysis is in order in connection with
the second branch. Once again, it is my intention to be brief.

(a) Rational connection

[
248
] Assuming that part of what constitutes the purpose of marriage is to
foster and provide institutional support for adult relationships that allow for
the possibility of procreation and child-rearing -- the restriction against
same- sex marriage, I find, [page443] is not rationally connected to this
objective. There simply is no evidentiary basis to support the proposition that
granting same-sex couples the freedom to marry would either diminish the number
of children conceived by heterosexual couples, or reduce the quality of care
with which heterosexual couples raise their children.

[
249
] Same-sex couples experience and raise children as a result of a
variety of reproductive and parenting arrangements, none of which is unique to
same-sex partners. Both same-sex and heterosexual couples foster children,
adopt children, conceive children by means of assisted conception and
surrogacy, and form blended families with children from previous relationships.
The fact that many heterosexual couples also conceive children through
heterosexual intercourse is not, I find, a rational basis for distinguishing
between all heterosexual and same-sex couples by granting only the former
access to the institutional supports of marriage. [See Note 140 below]

[
250
] I would agree with the submission, and I find that the restriction
against same-sex marriage fails the rational connection test because it is
both:

-- overinclusive in that it allows non-procreative
heterosexuals to marry; and

-- underinclusive because it denies same-sex
parents and intended parents the right to marry. [See Note 141 below]

(b) Degree of impairment

[
251
] The objective for the court under this part of the test is to decide
whether the impugned law impairs the rights of the applicants as little as
reasonably possible. I find that the denial to lesbians and gays of the right
to marry does not minimally impair their equality rights. Indeed -- as I have
already found -- what the law does do is exclude them entirely as a class of
persons based upon a protected personal characteristic.

[
252
] The AGC argues that in the present case, there does not appear to be
any other way to achieve Parliament's objective than by its support and
recognition of that definition of marriage as reflected in the common law and
which has been re- confirmed by
MBOA
. It goes on to submit that the means
chosen by the government -- sustaining the opposite-sex meaning of marriage
while extending equal treatment to same-sex relationships -- [page444]
infringes the applicants' rights as little as reasonably possible. It concludes
by submitting that this court should therefore defer to the views of
Parliament.

[
253
] In my opinion -- and specific to this issue -- I do not find this to
be an appropriate case for this court to pay deference to the views of
Parliament. On the fundamental issue before this court, Parliament has not
expressed its views in any fashion that would ordinarily provoke the issue of
judicial deference. I come to this conclusion for two reasons.

[
254
] First -- as I have already concluded above -- Parliament has chosen
not to exercise its legislative jurisdiction over capacity to marry. Rather,
the best that can be said is that it has only asserted its view in the
MBOA

while at the same time clearly stating that the definition of marriage was not
being addressed in the legislation. [See Note 142 below] This leads me to the
second reason which is -- in the absence of legislation it is principally the
court's responsibility and function to address issues that arise out of the
common law.

[
255
] I respectfully disagree with the submission of the AGC that the role
of the legislature "demands deference" from the courts for those
complex social policy decisions that the legislature is best able to make. Far
from demanding, I would point out that our Supreme Court has stated on several
occasions that:

[w]hile decisions of our legislatures may be
entitled to deference under s. 1 [of the
Charter
] as a matter of policy, such
deference is not required where we are being asked to review a law that we as
judges have established. [See Note 143 below]

(My emphasis)

[
256
] I interpret such guidance from our Supreme Court as being stated in
the permissive sense and not declaratory as suggested by the AGC. I believe
this to be the case even if this court were to conclude that Parliament has
expressed a "decision" in connection with capacity to marry. In any
event, as I have found, there is no "decision" of Parliament to
consider. And -- given that this court is being asked to "review a law
that we as judges have established" -- it is my opinion that deference is
to Parliament is not appropriate. I will have more to say on this below.

(c) Balance [of] deleterious and salutary effects

[
257
] Under this heading, the court is to decide "whether the
consequences of the violation are too great when measured [page445] against the
benefits that may be achieved". [See Note 144 below] In that regard, the
benefits to be achieved, says the AGC, include the assertion that the societal
concerns relating to marriage -- being the foundational institution in modern
society -- are extremely complex. They add that when such benefits are measured
against the exclusion of gays and lesbians from the institution, the
consequences to gays and lesbians are not too great.

[
258
] The essence of the AGC's submissions on the issue of deleterious
effects on gays and lesbians is centred on the notion that the marginalization
and historical disadvantage suffered by gays and lesbians has not been caused
by their legal incapacity to marry. Rather, it says, the prejudice they have
suffered has not been directed at them because they are not able to marry --
but because of societal attitudes towards homosexuality.

[
259
] The AGC adds that the benefits that gays and lesbians have
historically been denied as a result of exclusion from marriage have now been
provided by federal legislation and in some provinces to same-sex couples.
Because of the provision of the material benefits of marriage, the AGC contends
that the argument of the applicants as to the deleterious effects of exclusion
is condensed to mere recognition that is presently afforded to opposite-sex
couples.

[
260
] As I have now found on several occasions in these reasons, that
proposition is simply wrong. To repeat, this is not a case that simply involves
nomenclature, and even if it can be said that it is about "mere
recognition" -- the recognition in question that is being sought is for
equality. The essence of what the AGC claims to already exist, and which it
says amounts to legislative recognition of gay and lesbian unions -- really
imports nothing more than tolerance -- it is not the equal of full acceptance.

[
261
] In the case at bar, just as in the case of Vriend, "the
deleterious effects of the exclusion . . . are numerous and clear." [See
Note 145 below] The restriction against same-sex marriage is an offence to the
dignity of lesbians and gays because it limits the range of relationship
options available to them. The result is they are denied the autonomy to choose
whether they wish to marry. This in turn conveys the ominous message that they
are unworthy of marriage. For those same-sex couples who do wish to marry, the
impugned restriction represents a rejection of their personal aspirations and
the denial of their dreams.

[
262
] There is no meaningful evidence that points to any legitimate benefit
to the rights denial. In this case, an absolute common [page446] law bar on the
freedom of same-sex couples to marry does not constitute the "least
intrusive" means by which the state could achieve the purported goal of
providing institutional support to couples who have and raise children. On the
contrary, this goal could easily be advanced without denying same-sex couples
the freedom to marry.

[
263
] Further, I find that there is no merit to the argument that the rights
and interests of heterosexuals would be affected by granting same-sex couples
the freedom to marry. Contrary to the assertion of Interfaith Coalition -- I
cannot conclude that freedom of religion would be threatened or jeopardized by
legally sanctioning same-sex marriage. No religious body would be compelled to
solemnize a same-sex marriage against its wishes and all religious people -- of
any faith -- would continue to enjoy the freedom to hold and espouse their
beliefs. Thus, there is no need for any infringement of the equality rights of
lesbians and gays that arises because of the restrictions against same-sex marriage.

[
264
] In this case, I am satisfied that, even if the exclusion of same-sex
couples from marriage recognition were otherwise appropriate, the harms of
exclusion are so severe that the violation of their rights and freedoms could
not be justified. Given the serious violation of fundamental rights and
freedoms, and the evidence of numerous and damaging effects to an already
disadvantaged segment of society, I can find no benefit whatsoever to the
exclusion.

[
265
] For the above stated reasons -- and if the second part of the Oakes
test was a requirement -- the infringement of the applicants'
s. 15

Charter

rights is not proportional to the stated objective. I find that the
infringement of the applicants' Charter rights cannot be justified under
s. 1

of the Charter.

[
266
] I now turn to the last issue -- and perhaps the most troublesome
aspect of these applications -- the remedy.

(vi) What is the Appropriate Remedy?

[
267
] As I said, this is perhaps the most troublesome aspect of this
decision and it is the one that has caused me some of my most worrisome
moments. My worries do not come from not knowing what the correct remedy is --
I know full well what that is. Rather, they flow from the question of who is,
or ought to be, responsible for providing the remedy? On this issue I have had
the opportunity of reading and considering the decisions of my two colleagues,
Smith A.C.J. and Blair R.S.J. And, I agree completely with Blair R.S.J. where
he states that in connection with the appropriate remedy -- it is most
difficult.

[
268
] Smith A.C.J. and Blair R.S.J. have both concluded -- as I have -- that
the present common law definition of marriage is [page447] constitutionally
invalid and inoperative. In addition, they have each concluded that the proper
remedy is to suspend the operation and declaration of invalidity of the common
law rule for a period of 24 months. This is said to be necessary to enable
Parliament and legislatures the opportunity to correct the violation and bring
the impugned law into line with the constitutional requirements of the
Charter
.

[
269
] Smith A.C.J. proposes that the judiciary will be then more able to
respond if Parliament fails to act within that 24- month period. Her view,
expressed in para. 17 of her reasons, is that "the court will be in a much
better position at that time to make the appropriate evaluation of the relevant
societal circumstances than the court is today". Thus, if Parliament and
the legislature fail to act within the allotted time, then the issue can be returned
to this court for further consideration and action.

[
270
] Blair R.S.J., on the other hand, would declare a reformulated common
law definition of marriage to be in force and effect at the expiry of the
24-month period. Among other things, he maintains in para. 133 of his reasons,
that "there are other alternatives that might be weighed in determining
how marriage -- or the institution in present day Canadian society that will
afford full and equal recognition to same-sex couples as marriage presently does
to opposite-sex couples -- is to be redefined, or reformulated" (original
emphasis).

[
271
] However, in spite of my two learned colleagues' very well reasoned and
compelling decisions on this point, I very respectfully disagree with each of
them.

[
272
] I begin my analysis with a restatement of
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
, which provides that:

52(1) The Constitution of Canada is the supreme
law of Canada, and any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the
Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency, of no force and effect.

[
273
] As I noted at the beginning of question (iii) above, this court has
two options when considering what remedy should be applied to these
applications:

-- First is to measure the common law definition of
marriage against the
Charter
or constitutional values. Such an approach does
not require any constitutional remedy as prescribed by
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982. That is, it is not necessary for this court to hold
that the common law rule is of "no force and effect". Application of
this option would simply require reformulating the common law rule by reading
out the words "a man and a woman" and reading in "two persons".

-- Second is to apply
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
and make a declaration of invalidity. In my opinion, to apply this
[page448] approach invites the enigma wherein Canada would be potentially left
with no common law definition for marriage. One can only begin to imagine the
mischief this would cause.

[
274
] It has been argued that, as part of the option of remedy under s.
52(1), this court could also suspend the declaration of invalidity for a period
of time to enable Parliament to legislate in conformity with the
Charter
. While
this is the remedy that was decided upon by my two colleagues, respectfully I
am not at all certain that this court has such authority given that, in large
part there is no statute to read-down, read-in, or amend.

[
275
] The AGC submits that given the independent yet complementary
constitutional jurisdiction over marriage and matters related to marriage, any
gaps in the provincial or federal spheres should not be remedied through a
change in one legislative sphere. Because of this, it is said, any remedy in
this case should be fashioned through consultations between the two levels of
government and not by the court. In that regard, the AGC once again submits
that this court should defer the matter to Parliament and the provincial
legislatures.

[
276
] The applicants argue that the most fitting and fair remedy is for this
court to reformulate the common law rule. They contend that a s. 52(1)
Constitution Act order of invalidity is not appropriate. Furthermore, they
argue that if a declaration of invalidity is made, there should be no
suspension granted because the only remedy that will comply with the
Charter
is
"full and equal marriage recognition".

[
277
] For me, the central point of analysis must begin with the purpose that
-- where the guarantee of equality has been denied -- the remedy selected must
promote "a society in which all are secure in the knowledge that they are
recognized at law as human beings equally deserving of concern, respect, and
consideration". [See Note 146 below] Our Supreme Court has previously
voiced this purpose in Corbière v. Canada (Minister of Indian and Northern
Affairs):

In selecting an appropriate remedy under the

Charter
the primary concern of the court must be to apply the measures that
will best vindicate the values expressed in the Charter and to provide the form
of remedy to those whose rights have been violated that best achieves that
objective. This flows from the court's role as guardian of the rights and
freedoms which were entrenched as part of the supreme law of Canada. [See Note
147 below] [page449]

[
278
] However, I accept that any approach that I take must be measured with
an eye to the role of our elected lawmakers. A major revision of legal rules,
including the common law, with complex or uncertain ramifications, it is said
is best left to the legislatures. The Supreme Court in Watkins v. Olafson
explained the need for judicial caution as follows:

There are sound reasons supporting this judicial
reluctance to dramatically recast established rules of law. The court may not
be in the best position to assess the deficiencies of the existing law, much
less problems which may be associated with the changes it might make. The court
has before it a single case; major changes in the law should be predicated on a
wider view of how the rule will operate in the broad generality of cases.
Moreover, the court may not be in a position to appreciate fully the economic
and policy issues underlying the choice it is asked to make. Major changes to
the law often involve devising subsidiary rules and procedures relevant to
their implementation, a task which is better accomplished through consultation
between courts and practitioners than by judicial decree. Finally, and perhaps
most importantly, there is the long-established principle that in a
constitutional democracy it is the legislature, as the elected branch of
government, which should assume the major responsibility for law reform. [See
Note 148 below]

(My emphasis)

[
279
] And, while it may be the case that authorities such as Watkins v.
Olafson did not involve
Charter
considerations in connection with the common
law rule in issue, nonetheless their application in the within case is found in
the Supreme Court's note of caution and guidance. Thus, courts must consider
how the revised law will impact generally as opposed to only in the instant
case. In addition, a court should ask itself whether it is able to appreciate
the economic and political ramifications of the amendment. And, the court
should also examine the question of whether it is law reform that is best left
to the legislature.

Deference to the legislatures

[
280
] As I have noted at several points throughout these reasons, the AGC
argues that a key consideration in this case is that virtually all the alleged
benefits and obligations of marriage flow from the adoption of marriage in
specific legislation and not from the common law definition itself. It adds
that the Supreme Court has recognized that the pursuit of equality in the
distribution of benefits and obligations flowing from consenting and committed
marriage-like relationships does not require conflation of the meaning or
essence of marriage as a special kind of monogamous [page450] opposite-sex
union. [See Note 149 below] This same principle has found favour with and been
applied by courts in the United States.

[
281
] The Vermont Supreme Court recently found in the case of Baker v. State
that the need to ensure equality of benefits and protections between married
couples and same-sex couples did not require a re-definition of marriage. The
court held that it only required that the legislator craft a solution that made
such benefits and protections available to same-sex couples. The means by which
that was accomplished was left to the legislature. The notion of marriage in
the State of Vermont remained, and still remains, unchanged. [See Note 150
below]

[
282
] For reasons that I have already set out above, I reject this argument.
To repeat, it is my view that any "alternative status" that
nonetheless provides for the same financial benefits as marriage in and of
itself amounts to segregation. This case is about access to a deeply meaningful
institution -- it is about equal participation in the activity, expression,
security, and integrity of marriage. Any "alternative" to marriage,
in my opinion simply offers the insult of formal equivalency without the

Charter
promise of substantive equality. Again, an "alternative" I
find will only provide a demonstration of society's tolerance -- it will not
amount to a recognized acceptance of equality.

[
283
] Another argument of the AGC is that any expansion by the court would
irrevocably change the nature of marriage in our society, contradict the
legislative intention and displace the role of Parliament and the legislatures
and thus, constitute an excessive intrusion into the legislative sphere. Once
again, I am of the opinion that Parliament has only noted its view of what the
common law definition of marriage is -- it has not "unequivocally chosen
to reaffirm the meaning of marriage as a union of a man and a woman". [See
Note 151 below]

[
284
] There is little in the way of reliable evidence in this matter that
shows that a fundamental change to the definition of marriage would likely
affect those other laws relating to marriage. I do not disagree with Blair
R.S.J. when he concludes that the consequences and potential reverberations
flowing from a new definition of marriage will be first perceived as complex.
Moreover, I have little doubt that, as Blair R.S.J. notes in para. 97 of his
reasons, "they will touch the core of many people's belief [page451] and
value systems, and their resolution is laden with social, political, cultural,
emotional and legal ramifications".

[
285
] However -- and although I might be inclined to accept Blair R.S.J.'s
expression of possible ramifications -- they are nonetheless observations that
are made in the absence of satisfactory evidence. This is equally the case, I
say most respectfully, to the view of Smith A.C.J. set out in para. 10 of her
reasons where she finds that, "there are a myriad of legislative responses
that Parliament and the provincial legislature will have to consider to fill
the lacunae resulting from a declaration of constitutional invalidity of the
common law definition of marriage."

[
286
] In my view, what this court has before it is not evidence but rather
it is merely speculation, supposition and unsubstantiated opinion -- although
no doubt very honestly held. This is equally true for the proposition that a
change in the definition will affect the recognition abroad of Canadian
marriages; the various provincial requirements for solemnization; and every
federal and provincial statute and regulation that grants benefits and
obligations based on the current concept of marriage.

[
287
] However, I also believe that common sense still suggests that these
concerns -- even without any real evidentiary basis -- are sincerely and
genuinely held by those who proffer them. Indeed, most of these same arguments
were issues of concern to, and were considered by, the Supreme Court in M. v.
H. [See Note 152 below] It seems that it is just and prudent that this court
should seriously consider whether the legislatures ought to be given some
margin to address these questions in a more and all-inclusive fashion. To this
end, I have done so.

Reformulate the common law rule

[
288
] The Interfaith Coalition argues that the changes sought by the
applicants to the common law rule of marriage are more than incremental and
therefore should not be considered by this court. Specifically, it submits that
the courts have made it clear that the development of the common law that
involves changes to "general principles" or having significant or
complex legal ramifications should be left to Parliament.

[
289
] Pittfield J. in EGALE was of the opinion that the remedy sought by the
applicants in that case went far beyond the concept of acceptable common law
incremental change. Relying on Salituro he concluded that there are
restrictions on courts when considering changes to the common law.
Specifically, he reached this [page452] conclusion with reference to a passage
from the Supreme Court's decision where it said:

The common theme of the cases is that, while
complex changes to the law with uncertain ramifications should be left to the
legislature, the courts can and should make incremental changes to the common
law to bring legal rules into step with a changing society. [See Note 153
below]

[
290
] In the end, Pittfield J. concluded that the changes were more than
incremental and more appropriately should be deferred to the legislature to
consider. [See Note 154 below] My colleague, Blair R.S.J. as well agrees that
the changes being sought to the common law rule are more than incremental.
Indeed, he is of the opinion that to make the change sought through mere
re-wording would be to "strip the word 'incremental' of its meaning".
Once again, and with the utmost respect, I disagree.

[
291
] As for the changes proposed by the applicants being more than
incremental, it is of note that the only aspect of the original Hyde v. Hyde
and Woodmansee definition that apparently remains is "one man and one
woman". Briefly, there is no longer an exclusive issue of
"voluntary" in that many customs allow for arranged marriages. The
portion "for life" is both a long lost requirement and is somewhat
incompatible with the "divorce" portion of
s. 91(26)
of the

Constitution Act, 1867
.

[
292
] Finally, as for the economic and social issues described by Pittfield
J. in EGALE, [See Note 155 below] many, and perhaps most of those have been
addressed by our courts in cases such as Vriend and M. v. H. and by the
legislatures in response. For that matter, the core of the argument of the AGC
is that most, and potentially all of the economic benefits have or will be
addressed by other legislation. What then, I find myself asking, remains to be
considered? What is there that continues to be cautious about?

[
293
] I am acutely mindful of the very considered views of my colleagues
when they express concern for issues such as filiation links and international
recognition. And, that to change the common law definition of marriage will
upset the proper balance between judicial and legislative action. Again with
the greatest of respect, such concerns are simply not impacted by the capacity
to marry alone and are all issues very capable of being acted upon by
Parliament in any event. To make capacity to marry dependent upon such
expressed concerns is to my mind tantamount to having the tail wag the dog.
[page453]

[
294
] The common law rule of marriage is not itself a complex law -- indeed
it is straightforward and simple. In the final analysis, it does no more than
define who may participate in the societal institution of marriage. Thus, this
common law rule by definition is itself only a definition. That is, it defines
who has the capacity to marry. In my opinion, the change in issue in the within
case is incremental -- although its impact may be -- as many genuinely believe
-- very profound. In any case, it is my opinion that the issue of whether the
change is incremental or profound, as it might otherwise apply to the within
case, is an unworkable principle.

[
295
] The
Charter
breach in connection with the impugned common law rule can
only be remedied in one fashion, if it is appropriate that this court do so.
The choice is to amend it to include gays and lesbians -- as I believe it must
-- or to not amend it at all. There simply is no other amendment that could
otherwise be considered more incremental that this court can consider that will
achieve what is clearly the appropriate and correct remedy.

[
296
] If my decision is perceived as an encroachment into the Parliamentary
and legislative domains, then each court since that time long ago when a court
first developed the common law rule has also done the same. In Canada, since
1867 it has fallen upon the exclusive function of the courts to redefine
marriage from time to time as society evolved because Parliament chose -- for
whatever reasons -- not to do so within its sole constitutional jurisdiction.

[
297
] It is the courts that create the common law -- as they did in
connection with marriage -- and thereafter they are the guardians of that law.
Included within that: after first formulating a common law rule, the courts
will then be called upon to reformulate it from time to time so that it meets
the expanding demands and requirements of society. The court's role as the
guardian of such law is then only effectively usurped when the elected
legislature chooses to lawfully occupy the field. At such a point, the court's
role changes from that of guardian of the common law to guardian of
constitutional values.

[
298
] To this point in time Parliament has made the choice to not legislate
in connection with "capacity" to marry pursuant to
s. 91(26)
of the

Constitution Act, 1867
. In fact, contrary to the submission of the AGC that a
reformulation of the law by this court would displace the role of Parliament
and the legislatures -- it would not. Historically it has been left to the
courts to exclusively define marriage through the common law -- not Parliament.
Furthermore, the issues that are offered as being affected by a reformulation
of the common law are not part of the law of marriage but rather, they are the
products of other laws, namely, legislation passed by Parliament and the
legislatures. [page454]

[
299
] Indeed, Parliament may still exercise its jurisdiction regardless of
this court's decision and it can reshape it if it believes I am wrong. Because
of that, this decision can in no way be seen to be interfering with
Parliament's exclusive jurisdiction, and Parliament continues to be more than
able to legislate -- if and when it chooses to. The only caution is that any
such legislation will be subject to the same analysis as that just conducted in
the foregoing.

[
300
] There is, I believe, a distinction that can be made in the authorities
that are relied upon in respect of this issue. Among common law
Charter
cases
there are two distinct lines of decisions. The first involve those instances
where there is no constitutionally impugned government action but the common
law is developed in accordance with Charter values. For example, in R. v.
Salituro [See Note 156 below] and R. v. Hawkins [See Note 157 below], the court
was concerned with the common law rule that produced the result that a female
spouse was an incompetent witness against her husband in criminal proceedings.

[
301
] The second line of cases is those that involve government action done
in reliance on a common law rule that breaches
Charter
rights. For example, in
Dagenais v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp. [See Note 158 below] the court was
concerned with the common law rule that granted judges the authority to issue
publication bans in court proceedings. And in Swain [See Note 159 below] it was
in connection with the common law rule that permitted the Crown to adduce
evidence of an accused's insanity in criminal proceedings.

[
302
] I agree that it is the second line of cases, namely, Dagenais and
Swain that provides the guidance for the analysis to be undertaken by me in the
within case. That is, governments deny same-sex couples marriage licences
because the common law rule restricts the granting of such licences to opposite-sex
couples. Thus, I have undertaken the remainder of my analysis in conformity
with the guidance provided by authorities such as Dagenais and Swain.

[
303
] Having found that the common law rule and its definition of marriage
breach the applicants'
s. 15(1)

Charter
rights to be treated equally, it seems
to me that the authorities virtually require that a new common law rule must be
reformulated. As I noted above, in Swain the court's view was that, where the
analysis involves a Charter challenge to a common law, judge-made rule, the
Charter analysis is different than if it were a challenge [page455] to a
legislative provision. In such an instance, the court held, it is appropriate
to consider an alternative common law rule that would not be contrary to the
principles of the Charter. [See Note 160 below]

[
304
] The caveat is that in the reformulation, the new rule must be
thoroughly tested against the values set out in the
Constitution Act, 1982
, and
in particular it must meet the requirements of the Charter.

[
305
] In this case, having concluded that the common law bar on same-sex
marriage offends the
Charter
, I must now ask -- what new rule should be stated
that would survive Charter scrutiny? Given that the remedy must vindicate the
rights and guarantees infringed, the issue seems simple in terms of what
options are available. The new common law rule must be that same-sex couples
are free to legally marry. However, before concluding, I wish to make two
points.

[
306
] First, I do not accept that some form of legislative response to this
issue that goes about implementing the denied rights of the applicants in some
piecemeal form is appropriate. Such an approach is improper given the nature of
the rights denied, and I would agree with the comments of Iacobucci J. when he
considered a not dissimilar issue in Vriend. After concluding that
"governmental incrementalism" was not a suitable approach for
Charter

violations, he added:

In my opinion, groups that have historically been
the target of discrimination cannot be expected to wait patiently for the
protection of their human dignity and equal rights while governments move
toward reform one step at a time. If the infringement of the rights and
freedoms of these groups is permitted to persist while governments fail to
pursue equality diligently, then the guarantees of the
Charter
will be reduced
to little more than empty words. [See Note 161 below]

[
307
] Second, it is my firm opinion that there is absolutely no reason why
the rights infringements that are in issue -- and that have historically
persisted for gays and lesbians -- should continue any longer. On this point I
can say it no better than by echoing and adopting the profound and famous words
of Martin Luther King Jr., who, in 1963, wrote from the jail cell he then
occupied:

We must use time creatively, in the knowledge
that the time is always ripe to do right. . . . Now is the time to lift our
national policy from the quicksand of injustice to the solid rock of human
dignity. [See Note 162 below] [page456]

[
308
] In the end I find that "right" is achieved by the decision
that -- the common law rule that defines marriage as being, "the lawful
union of one man and one woman to the exclusion of all others" is
unconstitutional and must be reformulated. I further find that it is
"right" that this common law definition should be reformulated to
state that marriage is "the lawful union of two persons to the exclusion
of all others".

CONCLUSION

[
309
] For all of the foregoing reasons, I find that the answers to the
questions first posed by the applicant Couples as set out above [See Note 163
below] and reviewed herein, establish that gays and lesbians have been, and
continue to be, denied the freedom to marry each other. Further, I find that,
this exclusion from this fundamental social institution is due to the sexual
orientation of gays and lesbians who are an already disadvantaged group. Such
exclusion, I find, is unconstitutional in that it violates
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter of Rights
and Freedoms. In particular, I find that:

1. There is no statutory impediment to the issuance
of marriage licences to the applicant Couples or other same-sex couples who
otherwise meet the requisite criteria;

2. There is a common law rule that bars the
issuance of marriage licences to same-sex couples, namely, the definition of
marriage as the union of "one man and one woman to the exclusion of all
others";

3. The common law rule that bars gays and lesbians
from entering into the societal institution of marriage infringes the applicants'

s. 15(1)

Charter
rights to equal benefit of the law.

4. The
Charter
infringement cannot be saved by
s. 1

of the Charter. That is, it cannot be demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society. The exclusion of same-sex couples from the right to marry
serves no identifiable pressing, or legitimate, governmental objective.

5. This is not an appropriate case where the court
ought to pay deference to Parliament. The common law bar to marriage between
persons of the same sex ought to be reformulated by this court in order to
conform with
Charter
values, namely, it should be, "two persons to the
exclusion of all others"; [page457]

6. Marriage licences should issue to the applicant
Couples. Moreover, I declare that the marriages of Kevin Bourassa and Joe
Varnell and of Elaine Vautour and Anne Vautour are valid legal marriages. I
order that the Registrar General is required to accept registration of the
documents evidencing these two marriages.

[
310
] On the issue of costs, the applicants in both applications are
entitled to their costs on a partial indemnity scale. If the parties are unable
to agree upon the amounts, this court may be spoken to. The parties are
reminded that none of the intervenors are entitled to claim or be awarded costs
as against the other parties.
